SAMoE-VLA: A Scene Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts Vision-Language-Action Model for Autonomous Driving

Zihan You Affiliation: Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University Affiliation: School of Instrument Science and Engineering, Southeast University    Hongwei Liu Affiliation: Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University Affiliation: Zhili College, Tsinghua University    Chenxu Dang Affiliation: Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence and Automation, Huazhong University of Science and Technology    Zhe Wang Affiliation: Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University    Sining Ang Affiliation: Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University Affiliation: Department of Automation, University of Science and Technology of China    Aoqi Wang Affiliation: Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University Affiliation: Department of Automation, University of Science and Technology Beijing    Yan Wang ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University
Abstract

Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising capabilities in autonomous driving by leveraging the understanding and reasoning strengths of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, our empirical analysis reveals that directly applying existing token-level MoE mechanisms—which are inherited from LLM architectures—to VLA models results in unstable performance and safety degradation in autonomous driving, highlighting a misalignment between token-based expert specialization and scene-level decision-making. To address this, we propose SAMoE-VLA, a scene-adaptive Vision-Language-Action framework that conditions expert selection on structured scene representations instead of token embeddings. Our key idea is to derive the MoE routing signal from bird’s-eye-view (BEV) features that encapsulates traffic scene context, enabling scenario-dependent expert weighting and merging tailored to distinct driving conditions. Furthermore, to support temporally consistent reasoning across world-knowledge, perception, language, and action, we introduce a Conditional Cross-Modal Causal Attention mechanism that integrates world state, linguistic intent, and action history into a unified causal reasoning process. Extensive experiments on the nuScenes open loop planning dataset and LangAuto closed-loop benchmark demonstrate that SAMoE-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming prior VLA-based and world-model-based approaches with fewer parameters. Our code will be released soon.

Keywords: 
Mixture of Expert VLA Autonomous Driving

1 Introduction

End-to-end autonomous driving, which aims to generate vehicle trajectories directly from raw sensor inputs, has achieved significant progress [18, 14, 39, 28, 46]. Supported by large-scale datasets and unified optimization objectives, these approaches produce driving behaviors that are both effective and smooth, achieving near–human-level performance in certain scenarios. However, when facing diverse urban layouts or unexpected interactions, these systems still lack the reasoning flexibility of human drivers [5]. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) [13, 2, 41, 6, 40, 29] and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) [19, 16, 53, 54] architectures extend this paradigm by introducing semantic reasoning and contextual understanding, enabling proactive decision-making. While most VLAs remain densely parameterized, the growing interest in conditional computation has motivated the adoption of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) ,which has been proven highly effective in large language models [13, 38], to improve scalability and specialization while reducing model parameter size.

In language modeling, token-level routing allows fine-grained expert specialization without violating structural constraints. In autonomous driving, however, decision-making is grounded in globally coupled scene semantics and temporally continuous world dynamics. Our experiments and empirical analysis in Fig. 4 indicate that token-level routing and discrete expert selection, as used in soft and sparse MoE, can disrupt temporal causality and cross-modal coordination in driving planning. In particular, token-level sparse MoE increases the collision rate by 38.4% compared to the dense baseline, resulting in inconsistent and unsafe trajectory generation in complex scenes. These findings suggest a granularity mismatch between token-level expert routing and scene-level embodied decision-making. Moreover, previous explorations for autonomous driving [49, 47] rely on manually defined router supervision, specialist annotations, and complex training regimes. While effective in controlled settings or benchmarks, such designs couple expert behavior with predefined skill partitions, which may limit scalability and adaptability to diverse interaction patterns.

From this observation, we derive two design principles for MoE in autonomous driving: (i) expert routing should be conditioned on structured scene context rather than individual tokens; (ii) cross-modal reasoning must preserve temporal causal consistency across world state, language intent, and action history.

Based on these principles, we propose SAMoE-VLA, a soft-weighted Mixture-of-Experts Vision-Language-Action model for scene-adaptive autonomous driving. Our Scene-Adaptive MoE(SA-MoE) performs differentiable expert fusion guided by bird’s-eye-view (BEV) scene representations that capture traffic geometry and interaction structure. This design enables coherent expert specialization at the scene level while maintaining smooth policy evolution. In addition, we introduce a Conditional Cross-Modal Causal Attention (CMCA) mechanism that unifies world, language, and planning representations under a temporally aligned causal mask, enabling consistent reasoning across modalities and time.

Experiments both on the nuScenes open loop planning dataset and LangAuto close loop benchmark show that SAMoE-VLA achieves state-of-the-art results while using fewer parameters as shown in figure 8, validating the benefits of BEV-based scene adaptive routing, soft-weight expert fusion, and causal world-language-action unification. We summarize our contributions as follows:

  • •

    We present SAMoE-VLA, a Mixture-of-Experts Vision-Language-Action framework that unifies the world, language, and planning spaces via a Conditional Cross-Modal Causal Attention mechanism.

  • •

    We introduce a BEV-guided Scene Adaptive MoE, routed by spatial traffic geometry captured from a lightweight Deformable Scene Encoder, enabling differentiable scene-aware expert fusion.

  • •

    Comprehensive experiments both on the nuScenes open loop planning dataset and LangAuto close loop benchmark demonstrate that SAMoE-VLA achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance over existing VLAs and world model approaches.

2 Related Work

2.1 VLA for End-to-End Autonomous Driving

Recent progress in large vision-language models (VLMs) has boosted their use in end-to-end autonomous driving. Zhou et al.[53] uses pre-trained VLMs for 3D-based driving actions with hierarchical alignment, leading in open-loop planning on nuScenes. Zhou et al.[54] adds action tokens to VLMs for policy learning, using adaptive reasoning and RL fine-tuning (GRPO) for better results. ORION [12] includes a QT-Former for history, an LLM for reasoning, and a planner for actions. jiang et al.[17] decouples VLM decisions (Senna-VLM) from E2E predictions (Senna-E2E). Li et al.[25] and Li et al.[24] apply RL to VLMs for better reasoning, using rewards from trajectories and actions. Advanced architectures like mixture-of-experts (MoE) handle variety. Yang et al.[49] adds MoE to vision and actions for multi-view and rare cases. Instead of selected views input or relaying on predefined router labels, our model utilizes the BEV as input to provide global perspective, employs world modeling through the proposed cross attention mechansim, and softly weight and fuse the scene adaptive MoE without any pre-labeled router.

2.2 Mixture of Experts

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) [4] architectures enable efficient and scalable model capacity expansion by employing a gating function that adaptively routes or weights expert activations. Shazeer et al.[38] pioneered the introduction of the sparsely-gated Mixture-of-Experts layer, which significantly reduce resource consumption. Later extensions [55, 20, 36, 21, 32], such as Switch Transformer [11] and GLaM [10], further refine this idea by simplifying routing, adding load-balancing losses and scaling to trillion-parameter regimes. Despite their success, sparse and Non-differentiable gating raises training instability [21, 35] and token dropping [1, 11, 55]. SoftMOE [34] illustrate soft assignment through mixing tokens to tackle those obstacles. Instead of merging tokens, SMEAR [33] and Lory [51] introduce expert merging to address the auto-regressive limitations often associated with SoftMOE. In this work, we aim to propose a scalable and unrestricted Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing mechanism specifically tailored for autonomous driving.

3 Method

In this section, we present the architecture and design details of our proposed SAMoE-VLA framework. We begin by describing the overall model architecture, followed by a detailed introduction to our Conditional Cross-Modal Causal Attention mechanism and soft weighted planning experts. Finally, we define our training objective and the specific training stages employed.

3.1 Method Architecture

Based on a pretrained large world vision language model [52] and post-trained flow matching-based planning expert, our model unifies world space, language space and action space through Conditional Cross-Modal Causal Attention(CMCA) across a mixture of functional experts. SAMoE-VLA, as depicted in Figure 1, comprises two main specialized functional experts across the transformer backbone: (1) A world-language expert that processes language tokens from human instruction, BEV tokens generated from BEV encoder [26] and groups of soft prompts derived from BEV features and combined with learnable embeddings; (2) a planning expert structured with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers that takes ego state tokens and noisy action tokens as inputs. Instead of relying on a single feed-forward network (FFN) with limited representational capacity to capture semantic reasoning, 3D geometry, and control information simultaneously, the use of specialized experts prevents the formation of overly blended or averaged representations.

World-Language Expert takes Bird’s-Eye View (BEV) representation as input and provides powerful spatial semantic understanding, instruction following, and reasoning capabilities. While previous works either restrict the input to particular camera viewpoints [54] or employ routers to select input views[49], which introduces security vulnerabilities, the use of BEV could provide a global perspective and avoid security challenges. This expert also accepts soft prompts as world tokens and enrich their representation to forecast future scenes 3D point clouds. The adoption of a World Vision-Language Model, in lieu of a common VLM, offers advantages by conferring the ability to predict future states and mitigating information losses typically associated with projection layer [22]. This capability is crucial for enabling the model to gain a comprehensive understanding of the generated driving behaviors and the subsequent consequences these actions may entail. Additional implementation details are provided in Appendix B.

Planning Expert structured with SA-MoE generates the planning trajectories via a flow matching mechanism, which further supervises the planning expert by requiring it to predict the velocity field that transports noisy intermediate actions toward ground-truth trajectories. Further details are provided in Section 3.3, Section 3.4 and Appendix A.

3.2 Conditional Cross-Modal Causal Attention

Conditional Cross-Modal Causal Attention, also known as CMCA, is designed to enable temporally causal action generation while conditioning on heterogeneous contextual modalities, including world, language, and ego-state representations. CMCA treats conditioning tokens as a temporally static and globally visible context that does not participate in the autoregressive update dynamics of action tokens. This asymmetric information flow ensures that contextual representations serve as stable memory sources rather than evolving sequence elements during action generation. Our conditional formulation decomposes the token sequence into two disjoint partitions: the conditioning context (BEV tokens, world tokens, language tokens, ego state tokens) and the action tokens to be generated. Let 𝐀∈0,1B×L×L\mathbf{A}\in{0,1}^{B\times L\times L} denote the binary attention mask, where 𝐀b,i,j=1\mathbf{A}_{b,i,j}=1 indicates that the ii-th token can attend to the jj-th token in the bb-th sequence. We define the mask as

𝐀b,i,j={1,j∈𝒞,1,i,j∈𝒜​ and ​j≤i,0,otherwise.\mathbf{A}_{b,i,j}=\begin{cases}1,&j\in\mathcal{C},\\ 1,&i,j\in\mathcal{A}\text{ and }j\leq i,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (1)

where 𝒞\mathcal{C} indexes the conditioning tokens shared across all autoregressive steps. This design allows every action token to attend to all conditioning tokens and its own historical actions while conditioning tokens neither attend to action tokens nor update through autoregressive decoding steps, thus realizing a temporally causal yet contextually grounded generation process.

To efficiently compute attention under structured visibility constraints, we integrate the masking operation directly into the similarity matrix prior to normalization. Specifically, the masked attention output is formulated as:

𝐎=softmax⁡(𝐒+(1−𝐀)⋅(−M))​𝐕,\mathbf{O}=\operatorname{softmax}\Big(\mathbf{S}+(1-\mathbf{A})\cdot(-M)\Big)\,\mathbf{V}, (2)

where 𝐀b,i,j∈{0,1}\mathbf{A}_{b,i,j}\in\{0,1\} denotes the structured visibility mask, and M→+∞M\rightarrow+\infty is a sufficiently large constant that effectively suppresses disallowed positions. Under this formulation, entries with 𝐀b,i,j=1\mathbf{A}_{b,i,j}=1 retain their original similarity scores, while entries with 𝐀b,i,j=0\mathbf{A}_{b,i,j}=0 are shifted toward negative infinity prior to the softmax operation, ensuring zero attention weight after normalization. 𝐕\mathbf{V} is represented as the concatenation results of each value states process from each domain expert. This causal alignment further ensures compatibility with the flow matching objective, which requires temporally coherent intermediate states to learn a smooth velocity field for trajectory refinement.

3.3 Scene Adaptive MoE with Deformable Scene Encoder

To endow the planning expert with adaptive and specialized decision-making abilities across diverse driving situations, We propose a Planning Expert based on a Scene-Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture. Unlike conventional dense FFNs that average diverse behavioral patterns into a single representation, Our design decomposes the policy into multiple sub-experts, each specializing in a subspace of driving behaviors, and the planning expert’s parameters during inference are dynamically weighted and fused based on different driving scenarios without any predefined labels. The key contribution lies in a soft BEV-guided scene adaptive expert routing mechanism which is both fully differentiable and dynamic according to the current traffic context.

Scene Adaptive Routing via Deformable Scene Encoding. Given a BEV feature map 𝐅BEV∈ℝB×H×W×C\mathbf{F}_{\text{BEV}}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times H\times W\times C}, we extract routing logits using a lightweight Deformable Scene Encoder, termed DSE. This module augments BEV features with a distance-guided deformable convolution to capture geometric and contextual cues of current traffic scenarios. Conventional convolutions apply a fixed kernel at each spatial location, assuming uniform information density across the feature map [8]. Such fixed sampling fails to capture the highly anisotropic spatial relevance present in driving scenes, so these critical features near the ego vehicle are sampled with the same density as far-away background pixels. This leads to semantic dilution and inefficient feature utilization when routing MoE experts. To solve this problem, we demonstrate the deformable encoding mechanism as follows.

Given 𝐅BEV∈ℝB×C×H×W\mathbf{F}_{\text{BEV}}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times C\times H\times W}, we generate spatial offsets 𝚫∈ℝB×2​K2×H×W\mathbf{\Delta}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times 2K^{2}\times H\times W} through a learned predictor conditioned on both BEV features and a normalized distance map 𝐌𝐧𝐞𝐚𝐫\mathbf{M_{near}}:

Mnear​(i,j)=1−dist⁡((i,j),(cx,cy))distmax∈[0,1],M_{\text{near}}(i,j)=1-\frac{\mathrm{dist}\!\left((i,j),(c_{x},c_{y})\right)}{\mathrm{dist}_{\max}}\in[0,1], (3)

where (cx,cy)(c_{x},c_{y}) is the ego-center of the BEV and K is the size of the convolutional kernel used in the deformable convolution. 𝐌𝐧𝐞𝐚𝐫\mathbf{M_{near}} attains higher values near the ego location, thereby serving as a near-field attention prior.

The offset field for deformable convolution is predicted by:

Δ=𝒫⁡([𝐅BEV;Mnear]),Δ∈ℝB×2​K2×Hc×Wc,\Delta=\mathcal{P}\left([\mathbf{F}_{\text{BEV}};M_{\text{near}}]\right),\quad\Delta\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times 2K^{2}\times H_{c}\times W_{c}}, (4)

where 𝒫⁡(⋅)\mathcal{P}(\cdot) is a small convolutional predictor initialized to zeros which ensures that the model begins with an identity convolution and gradually learns meaningful offset patterns during training. These learnable offsets allow the receptive field to dynamically adapt to scene geometry and local feature saliency, enabling the network to focus on semantically informative regions.

The deformable convolution operation aggregates features under the learned spatial shifts:

𝐒BEV=Norm​(Flatten​(DeformConv​(𝐅BEV,𝚫))),\mathbf{S}_{\text{BEV}}=\text{Norm}(\text{Flatten}(\text{DeformConv}(\mathbf{F}_{\text{BEV}},\mathbf{\Delta}))), (5)

capturing fine-grained geometry and semantic layouts across the driving scene. We then flatten and normalize the features to obtain a sequence representation 𝐒BEV∈ℝB×N×C\mathbf{S}_{\text{BEV}}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times N\times C} .

To extract routing-aware embeddings, We introduce learnable query vectors 𝐐∈ℝ1×T×C\mathbf{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times T\times C} and apply multi-head cross attention:

𝐇BEV=MHA​(𝐐,𝐒BEV,𝐒BEV),\mathbf{H}_{\text{BEV}}=\text{MHA}(\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{S}_{\text{BEV}},\mathbf{S}_{\text{BEV}}), (6)

yielding the BEV-guided hidden states 𝐇BEV∈ℝB×T×C\mathbf{H}_{\text{BEV}}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times C}, which summarize traffic semantics and spatial configurations relevant to driving decisions. For the entire planning expert, 𝐇BEV\mathbf{H}_{\text{BEV}} is computed only once through DSE outside the transformer layers, thus incurring almost no additional computation time.

Soft Expert Weighted and Fused. Previous works focus on LLM extending MoE by selecting tokens to the top-k expert or softly weighted the tokens to each experts[34]. While experiments in Figure 4 suggest these mechanism are ill-suited for autonomous driving as they introduce the higher probability of collision. Instead of token-level specialization, we employ a soft weighted strategy that softly weights and fuses the experts. To be more specific, we calculate the weight of each expert routed by the signals encoded in DSE and merge these experts into a single FFN. Given 𝐇BEV\mathbf{H}_{\text{BEV}} in each MOE layers, we compute routing logits as:

𝐫=Linear​(MeanPool​(𝐇BEV))∈ℝB×E,\mathbf{r}=\text{Linear}(\text{MeanPool}(\mathbf{H}_{\text{BEV}}))\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times E}, (7)

where EE is the number of experts. Softmax normalization yields the expert weights:

𝝅=softmax​(𝐫),πe=exp⁡(re)∑e′exp⁡(re′).\boldsymbol{\pi}=\text{softmax}(\mathbf{r}),\quad\pi_{e}=\frac{\exp(r_{e})}{\sum_{e^{\prime}}\exp(r_{e^{\prime}})}. (8)

Linear layer enables the expert weights in each MoE layer to be guided by not only current traffic scenario but also allowing flexible weighting based on the layer’s position. These weights determine the contribution of each expert to the final action embedding.

Each expert e∈{1,…,E}e\in\{1,\dots,E\} comprises a lightweight feed-forward transformation parameterized by {𝐖1(e),𝐖2(e),𝐖3(e)}\{\mathbf{W}_{1}^{(e)},\mathbf{W}_{2}^{(e)},\mathbf{W}_{3}^{(e)}\}, analogous to the MLPs in transformer blocks. For attention output 𝐎∈ℝB×L×C\mathbf{O}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times L\times C} generated from CMCA as shown in formula 2,

The Hidden states of planning expert is computed as:

𝐇plan\displaystyle\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{plan}} =𝐎[:Lp]+𝐑plan∗\displaystyle=\mathbf{O}{[:L_{p}]}+\mathbf{R_{\mathrm{plan}}^{*}} (9)

where LpL_{p} serves as the sum length of state tokens and action tokens for planning, 𝐎[:Lp]\mathbf{O}{[:L_{p}]} serves as the planning part of the attention output, 𝐑plan∗\mathbf{R_{\mathrm{plan}}^{*}} represents the residual connection,𝐇plan\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{plan}} represents the hidden states in planning expert.

We then calculate the weight of each expert and fuse these experts into a single FFN:

𝐖~i\displaystyle\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{i} =∑e=1Eπe​𝐖i(e),i∈{1,2,3}\displaystyle=\sum_{e=1}^{E}\pi_{e}\,\mathbf{W}_{i}^{(e)},\quad i\in\{1,2,3\} (10)

The merged FFN 𝐖~i\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{i} then replaces the original FFN layer and calculates the output embeds with the input of 𝐇plan\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{plan}}:

𝐇plan′\displaystyle\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{plan}}^{\prime} =σ⁡(𝐇plan​𝐖~1)⊙(𝐇plan​𝐖~3)​𝐖~2\displaystyle=\sigma(\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{plan}}\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{1})\odot(\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{plan}}\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{3})\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{2} (11)

where σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) denotes the activation function SiLU and ⊙\odot represents element-wise multiplication. Further theoretical analysis and mathematical proofs, including representation capacity, temporal causality stability, convergence advantages, and gradient stability of SAMoE, is provided in Appendix E. Computational efficiency and deployment analysis is presented in Appendix I, with corresponding pseudocode given in Appendix F.

3.4 Training Stages and Objective

We train SAMoE-VLA in two main stages with different training objectives. For the pretraining stage, the planning expert is frozen while the world-language expert is exclusively trained. This training is executed by masking all state and action tokens and proceeding through the sequential sub-steps outlined in [52]. The overall training objective for the pretraining stage combines language modeling loss for unified scene understanding and the point cloud reconstruction loss for world prediction. The flow-matching loss ℒflow​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{flow}}(\theta)used in final stage teaches the model to estimate velocity fields, guiding noisy action interpolations toward true action paths, all based on a multimodal setup 𝒞\mathcal{C} that includes BEV tokens, language inputs, world details, and ego-state data. It supports creating smooth distributions of actions, boosting the model’s skill in delivering accurate, situation-specific forecasts for step-by-step choices in changing settings. The final training stage is partitioned into two distinct steps. In the first step, the model is trained without the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer to ensure training stability. For the second step, the weights established during this initial phase are directly used to initialize the individual sub-expert weights within the soft-weighted MoE layer of the planning expert. We provide further training details and pseudo-code in Appendix D.1 and Appendix F.

4 Experiments

4.1 Datasets and Implementation Details

We evaluate SAMoE-VLA on challenging nuScenes [3] dataset which is a large-scale, comprehensive collection comprising 1,000 diverse driving scenes, recorded across different cities, and featuring a total of 280,000 meticulously annotated frames. In addition to nuScenes, we conduct closed-loop evaluation on the LMDrive dataset and the LangAuto benchmark[37] built on the CARLA simulator[9], which provide approximately 64K multimodal instruction–sensor–control clips collected across 8 towns under diverse weather and lighting conditions. LangAuto evaluates language-conditioned closed-loop driving by testing an agent’s ability to follow natural-language navigation and notice instructions across varying route lengths and adversarial settings.

The SAMoE-VLA architecture integrates OpenCLIP-ConvNext[7] as the base image encoder, employing a CPFPN[31] to generate multi-scale feature maps. Subsequently, BEVFormer is adopted as the Bird’s-Eye-View (BEV) encoder, which processes a single input frame and encodes the resultant BEV features to a dimension of 256 and a spatial resolution of 𝟐𝟎𝟎×𝟐𝟎𝟎\mathbf{200\times 200}. Further details about world-language expert align with [52]. The model is trained using 8 NVIDIA A800 GPUs. For the planning experts, the model parameters are initialized from the pre-trained InternVL2-2B. Motivated by the design in [11], We replace the feed-forward layer with our proposed SA-MoE layer at every fourth Transformer layer. Action tokens are embedded through a linear projection, fused with sinusoidal time embeddings (with minimum period 4×10−34\times 10^{-3} and maximum period 4.04.0), and subsequently processed by a lightweight MLP to capture temporal dependencies. During the final stages, we use full parameter fine-tuning instead of Lora with the learning rate of 1e-4. For flow matching, Gaussian noise 𝜺∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) and a time coefficient τ∼Beta​(1.5,1.0)\tau\sim\text{Beta}(1.5,1.0) (clamped to [0.001,0.999][0.001,0.999]) are sampled to form the noisy action representation. During inference, the ODE steps to produce the trajectories is 10. Additional implementation details about flow matching are provided in Appendix A.

4.2 Main Results

As shown in Table 1, SAMoE-VLA achieves the lowest average L2 error (0.29 m) under our open-loop evaluation protocol, outperforming the previous VLA state of the art and the world model–based approach PreWorld by a 7%7\% relative reduction. While SAMoE-VLA is not consistently the best at the 1-second horizon, this behavior reflects its planning-oriented design, which prioritizes scene-level consistency and long-horizon feasibility over short-term motion fitting. Consequently, its advantages become increasingly evident at longer horizons. In particular, SAMoE-VLA achieves a 3-second L2 error of 0.35 m, which is 15% lower than the best VLA baseline and 5% lower than the strongest world model–based method, demonstrating its effectiveness in mitigating long-horizon error accumulation. Most VLA-based approaches outperform traditional end-to-end planners, while world model–based methods further improve long-horizon accuracy. Importantly, SAMoE-VLA maintains a favorable accuracy–safety trade-off, achieving the best average collision rate of 0.26%, outperforming world model–based and traditional planning methods. Qualitative results are provided in Appendix H.

Table 2 summarizes the closed-loop performance on LangAuto[37] under three evaluation settings. On the full LangAuto benchmark, SAMoE-VLA achieves the best Driving Score (51.4) and Route Completion (63.5), outperforming all 7B baselines while maintaining competitive instruction alignment. The advantage persists in LangAuto-Short, where SAMoE-VLA again ranks first in DS (69.5) and RC (80.9), demonstrating stronger short-horizon planning stability. Under LangAuto-Tiny, it attains the highest Instruction Score (0.92) while achieve the best Driving Score of 79.5, indicating robust language grounding in simplified scenarios. Despite its smaller parameter scale, SAMoE-VLA consistently delivers superior or balanced performance across execution quality and instruction compliance.

4.3 Ablation Study

Comparison to Existing MoE Mechanism. To examine the impact of different existing MoE Mechanism, we adopt five distinct baseline architectures. These baselines are systematically categorized into three groups based on their specialization approach: the non-MoE version, token-level specialization [38, 33], and expert-weighted specialization. As shown in figure 4, we find that deploying our soft-weighted SAMoE, which performs the best, could significantly decrease L2 error from 0.32 to 0.29 while nearly maintaining a moderate collision rate(0.25) compared with dense counterparts(0.25). Although the sparse routing mechanism could decrease L2 error from 0.32 to 0.30, it increases 38.4% of collision rate, thus raises a security challenge. Also, we observe that applying soft routing to action tokens severely degrades model performance, with the average L2 error increasing to 0.46 and the average collision rate rising to 0.57.

Additionally, to analyze the impact of the scene adaptive for token-based MoE routing, we implement two baseline that add additional routing bias derived from DSE. We find that incorporating scene bias into sparse MoE leads to a drastic performance drop, with the average L2 error rising to 0.57 and the collision rate reaching 0.69. The data further indicate a notable performance trade-off: incorporating scene bias into the soft-MoE architecture allows the model to nearly maintain the L2 error performance, yet it results in a detrimental effect on safety, evidenced by a significant increase in the collision rate to 0.34. The aforementioned results indicate that token-level routing is ill-suited for planning tasks in autonomous driving. Details and numerical results comparing with existing MoE approaches are provided in Appendix C, with a computational cost results in Appendix I.

Importance of scene adaptive routing Mechanism and DSE. Further experimentation is conducted to investigate the importance of DSE and driving scene adaptive routing by integrate additional baseline. As illustrated in Table 3, we first compare our scene adaptive routing strategy with an alternative prefix routing strategy. In prefix routing, expert merging is only guided by the first token of planning expert instead of BEV hidden vector captured by DSE. We find that the average L2 error for prefix routing is 0.31. While this demonstrates an improvement over Non-MoE version, its overall performance is inferior when compared directly to our proposed method by 6.8%. Deformable convolution network(DCN) is also removed to validate its necessity. Compared with our proposed method, L2 error is 0.31, which is also 6.8% lower. We also performed an ablation study by removing the normalized distance map (𝐌𝐧𝐞𝐚𝐫\mathbf{M_{near}}), which yielded a comparable, albeit slightly inferior, performance with an L2 error of 0.300.30 compared to our final model. The results above indicates the importance of our proposed scene adaptive routing mechanism and deformable scene encoder.

Impact of number of experts. We conduct experiments with different numbers of experts in our MoE architecture. As shown in Figure 6, we find that 12 experts produce the lowest L2 error of 0.28, outperforming other results, while 4 experts achieve the lowest collision rate of 0.26. The results indicate that employing either fewer or more experts than optimal fails to achieve notable performance improvements relative to the dense baseline model; only an appropriate number of experts can yield superior performance. We observe that fewer experts enhance robustness against collisions. 4 experts version significantly reduced the collision rate (0.26) compared to the two-expert version and the average collision rate exhibited a subsequent increase with the further growth in the total number of experts. Conversely, L2 errors decreases steadily with increasing number of experts, but 16 experts configuration performs the average L2 error of 0.33. These results underscore the importance of expert scaling in MoE designs for planning tasks, where excessive specialization (e.g., 16 experts) may introduce instability, while moderate scaling (4–12 experts) optimizes multi-objective performance.

Impact of Scene-Adaptive MoE on Challenging Scenarios. To further validate the scene-adaptive capability, we conducted an ablation study across three representative driving scenarios, which is selected from nuScenes: complex intersections, narrow-turn roads, and close-range overtaking. As shown in Figure 6, replacing the Scene adaptive MoE layer with a dense counterpart consistently leads to degraded planning accuracy and success rate across all settings. In complex intersections, the proposed soft weighted scene adaptive MoE reduces the average L2 distance from 0.33 m to 0.27 m and higher the success rate from 67.91% to 77.41%, indicating more stable trajectory prediction under high interaction density. The advantage becomes more pronounced in close-range overtaking, where the MoE version achieves a substantial reduction in average L2 (0.28 to 0.19 m) and 12% of success rate improvement, reflecting enhanced adaptability to rapidly changing relative motion. These results confirm that the scene-aware routing mechanism effectively allocates expert capacity according to environmental complexity. This experiment also serves as an empirical study of scene-level generalization, showing that the proposed SAMoE-VLA maintains stable planning quality across structurally distinct scenarios, demonstrating robustness in complex layouts. Due to space limitations, supplementary selection detiails are deferred to Appendix G.

Importance of Conditional Cross-Modal Causal Attention. We validate the importance of CMCA by introduce two additional experiments. Without employing a conditional autoregressive mechanism in which every action token could be seen by each other, our model will lead to an performance decline. The average L2 error exceed to 0.35, which indicates the success of our mask strategy. We also present a fully dense version where all the tokens (including BEV tokens and noisy action tokens) are processed in a single feed-forward layer in each transformer layer. Experiments for the fully dense version suggest L2 error is 0.03 higher compared with our baseline, showing the importance of specialized experts tailored to each distinct spatial application. To avoid interference, all the experiments have not deployed any SA-MoE layer.

Further experiment illustrate the importance of 3D-aware world modeling pretraining. Instead of training planning experts after future point cloud prediction, we simply finish the alignment steps and then train our planning expert. As shown in figure 8, we find that the average L2 error drop to 0.33, further implcates the role in world modeling.

Scene-Adaptive Route behavior Analysis via t-SNE. To further interpret the scene adaptive route’s behavior and its ability to classify traffic scenes, we visualize and cluster the hidden representations extracted from the Deformable Scene Encoder(DSE). Each sample-level feature vector is obtained by mean-pooling over the batch and temporal dimensions, followed by two-dimensional projection using t-SNE for local neighborhood visualization. Figure 4 illustrates that samples form several loosely separated clusters, with dense intra-cluster regions and partially overlapping boundaries, suggesting the presence of distinct yet related BEV scene patterns. These findings demonstrate that the DSE encodes semantically meaningful driving and traffic patterns, which correspond to distinct expert routing behaviors and provide evidence that the model’s soft-weighted MoE adapts dynamically to diverse scene contexts.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we introduce SAMoE-VLA, a scene-adaptive Mixture-of-Experts Vision-Language-Action model for Autonomous Driving. To address the limitations of dense architectures and token-level routing in existing VLA and MoE-based approaches, we proposed two key mechanisms: Conditional Cross-Modal Causal Attention (CMCA), which unifies world, language, and action representations, and a BEV-guided Scene Adaptive MoE (SA-MoE), which employs deformable scene encoding to achieve differentiable and driving-scene-aware expert fusion. Comprehensive experiments on both open and close planning benchmark demonstrate that SAMoE-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance, lower long-horizon prediction error, and superior robustness across complex driving scenarios, validating the effectiveness of soft expert weighting, scene adaptive routing, and world modeling based on CMCA.

SAMoE-VLA: A Scene Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts Vision-Language-Action Model for Autonomous Driving

Supplementary Material

A The implementation of Flow-Matching

Overview.

As illustrate in 3.3, we propose a conditional trajectory planning expert trained via flow matching. The system learns a time-conditioned velocity field to transport noise to ego-trajectory over a finite horizon.

A.1 Perception and Conditioning

Given multi-view images, a BEV encoder produces a tensor

𝐁∈ℝH×W×Cb.\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C_{b}}.

Deformable Scene Encoder 𝐃𝐒𝐄:ℝCb→ℝD\mathbf{DSE}:\mathbb{R}^{C_{b}}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{D} maps BEV feature to DD-dimensional tokens

𝐇BEV=𝐃𝐒𝐄⁡(reshape⁡(𝐁))∈ℝ(H​W)×D.\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{BEV}}=\mathbf{DSE}(\mathrm{reshape}(\mathbf{B}))\in\mathbb{R}^{(HW)\times D}.

We also embed auxiliary contexts: ego-history 𝐡\mathbf{h}, CAN bus 𝐜\mathbf{c}, and low-level control features 𝐥\mathbf{l} via linear projections

𝐒=concat⁡(ψhis​(𝐡),ψbus​(𝐜),ψego​(𝐥))∈ℝLs×D.\mathbf{S}=\mathrm{concat}\!\big(\psi_{\mathrm{his}}(\mathbf{h}),\;\psi_{\mathrm{bus}}(\mathbf{c}),\;\psi_{\mathrm{ego}}(\mathbf{l})\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{s}\times D}.

The overall conditioning is 𝒞={𝐳,𝐇bev,𝐒,𝐋,𝐖}\mathcal{C}=\{\mathbf{z},\mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{bev}},\mathbf{S},\mathbf{L},\mathbf{W}\}. Where the 𝐳\mathbf{z} denotes BEV tokens,𝐋\mathbf{L} denotes language instruction tokens , 𝐖\mathbf{W} denotes world tokens which are processed in world language expert.

A.2 Flow Matching Formulation

Let the planning horizon be KK, ground-truth future actions be

𝐚=(𝐚1,…,𝐚K)∈ℝK×da,da=2.\mathbf{a}=(\mathbf{a}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{a}_{K})\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d_{a}},\quad d_{a}=2.

where KK in NuScenes is 6. We sample noise and time as

ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈),t∼Beta⁡(α=1.5,β=1.0)⋅0.999+0.001.\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}),\qquad t\sim\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha{=}1.5,\beta{=}1.0)\cdot 0.999+0.001.

Define the convex interpolation and target velocity:

𝐱t=t​ϵ+(1−t)​𝐚,𝐮t=ϵ−𝐚.\mathbf{x}_{t}=t\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}+(1-t)\,\mathbf{a},\qquad\mathbf{u}_{t}=\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{a}.

We compute a sinusoidal time embedding γ⁡(t)∈ℝD\gamma(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{D} over periods [4×10−3, 4][4\times 10^{-3},\,4] and construct action–time tokens by projecting actions and fusing time:

𝐄act=ψact​(𝐱t)∈ℝK×D,𝐄time=γ⁡(t)​𝟏K∈ℝK×D,\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{act}}=\psi_{\mathrm{act}}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times D},\quad\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{time}}=\gamma(t)\mathbf{1}_{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times D},
𝐄suf=MLP([𝐄act∥𝐄time])∈ℝK×D.\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{suf}}=\mathrm{MLP}\big([\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{act}}\|\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{time}}]\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times D}.

The planning expert fθf_{\theta} consumes the concatenated sequence

𝐗=[𝐒∥𝐄suf]∈ℝ(Ls+K)×D,\mathbf{X}=\big[\mathbf{S}\;\|\;\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{suf}}\big]\in\mathbb{R}^{(L_{s}+K)\times D},

and outputs hidden states whose last KK positions are projected by ψout:ℝD→ℝda\psi_{\mathrm{out}}:\mathbb{R}^{D}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}} to produce the predicted velocity field vθv_{\theta}:

vθ​(𝐱t,t,𝒞)=ψout​(fθ​(𝐗)suffix)∈ℝK×da.v_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,\mathcal{C})=\psi_{\mathrm{out}}\big(f_{\theta}(\mathbf{X})_{\mathrm{suffix}}\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d_{a}}.
Training Objective.

The flow-matching loss aligns vθv_{\theta} with the target velocity:

ℒFM=1K​∑k=1K‖vθ​(𝐱t,t,𝒞)k−𝐮t,k‖22.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\big\|v_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,\mathcal{C})_{k}-\mathbf{u}_{t,k}\big\|_{2}^{2}. (12)

A.3 Inference via ODE Integration

At test time, we discard ground-truth actions and solve the transport from noise to actions by explicit Euler:

𝐱1∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈),Δ​t=−1N,t←1,\mathbf{x}_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}),\quad\Delta t=-\frac{1}{N},\quad t\leftarrow 1,
repeat N steps: 𝐱t+Δ​t←𝐱t+Δt⋅vθ(𝐱t,t,𝒞),t←t+Δt.\text{repeat }N\text{ steps: }\quad\mathbf{x}_{t+\Delta t}\leftarrow\mathbf{x}_{t}+\Delta t\cdot v_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,\mathcal{C}),\quad t\leftarrow t+\Delta t.

The final estimate 𝐚^=𝐱0∈ℝK×da\hat{\mathbf{a}}=\mathbf{x}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d_{a}} is the planned trajectory.

A.4 Implementation Details

(i) BEV features are linearly projected to DD-dimensional tokens and concatenated with state tokens to form 𝒞\mathcal{C}. (ii) Time embedding uses sine-cosine features with periods in [×10−3,4][4\!\times\!10^{-3},4]. (iii) Training samples (ϵ,t)(\boldsymbol{\epsilon},t) per batch; the planner predicts vθv_{\theta} over all KK steps, and the MSE in (12) is averaged across steps. (iv) For stability and efficiency, mixed precision and gradient checkpointing can be used.

B The implementation of World Modeling

Overview

Followed World language model HERMES[52], We adopted a world language expert that predicts future 3D scene geometry by rendering LiDAR rays from Large Language Model (LLM)-conditioned BEV features. Given BEV features via a BEV Encoder, compress them, and feed them into an LLM together with a compact set of learnable soft prompts. The LLM returns a refined current BEV embedding and future-aware soft world tokens, which we use to synthesize per-frame future BEV embeddings. We then lift each BEV into a unified voxel grid, and render depth along LiDAR rays to form predicted future point clouds. The full system is implemented with memory-efficient mixed-precision and gradient checkpointing. The expert is pretrained during first stage, and frozen in final stage.

Notation

Let the BEV spatial shape be (H,W)(H,W) and channel dimension CC. We denote the unified voxel grid by (Z,H,W)(Z,H,W) with vertical bins ZZ and per-voxel size Δ=(Δx,Δy,Δz)\Delta=(\Delta_{x},\Delta_{y},\Delta_{z}) covering a 3D range pc​_​range\mathrm{pc\_range}. We consider a frame set 𝒯={t,t+1,…,t+K}\mathcal{T}=\{t,t\!+\!1,\ldots,t\!+\!K\} where tt is current and K≥1K\!\geq\!1 is the number of future steps. For LiDAR rendering, a ray is a tuple (𝐨n,𝐝n,rn)(\mathbf{o}_{n},\mathbf{d}_{n},r_{n}), with origin 𝐨n∈ℝ3\mathbf{o}_{n}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{3}, unit direction 𝐝n∈ℝ3\mathbf{d}_{n}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{3}, and ground-truth range rn∈ℝ+r_{n}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}_{+} when available.

B.1 BEV Feature Extraction

From multi-view images, we compute the BEV embedding

𝐄t∈ℝHbev×Wbev×C\displaystyle\mathbf{E}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{H_{\mathrm{bev}}\times W_{\mathrm{bev}}\times C} (13)

using spatial cross attention(SCA) with learned queries and positional encodings:

𝐅B​E​V=SCA⁡(img_feats,BEV_queries,pos)\displaystyle\mathbf{F}_{BEV}=\mathrm{SCA}(\text{img\_feats},\text{BEV\_queries},\text{pos}) (14)

For LLM conditioning, we downsample BEV channels with a lightweight module DownSampleCross\mathrm{DownSampleCross} :

𝐳,𝐄tae=MLP⁡(DownSampleCross⁡(𝐅B​E​V)).\displaystyle\mathbf{z},~\mathbf{E}^{\mathrm{ae}}_{t}=\mathrm{MLP}(\mathrm{DownSampleCross}(\mathbf{F}_{BEV})). (16)

Here 𝐳\mathbf{z} is the LLM input representation and 𝐄tae\mathbf{E}^{\mathrm{ae}}_{t} is the reconstruction target for self-regularization when enabled.

B.2 LLM-guided Future BEV Generation

We compress 𝐳\mathbf{z} into NqN_{q} learnable queries by channel-wise pooling and add temporal/control priors:

𝐐\displaystyle\mathbf{Q} =Pool⁡(permute⁡(𝐳))∈ℝNq×C,\displaystyle=\mathrm{Pool}\big(\mathrm{permute}(\mathbf{z})\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{q}\times C}, (17)
𝐖(k)\displaystyle\mathbf{W}^{(k)} =𝐐+𝐟frame​(k),k∈{1,…,K},\displaystyle=\mathbf{Q}+\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{frame}}(k),\quad k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}, (18)

where 𝐟frame\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{frame}} is learnable soft prompt embeddings,𝐖(k)\mathbf{W}^{(k)} is the world tokens.

We feed the LLM with the downsampled BEV tokens and world tokens:

(𝐄tllm,{𝐐(k)}k=1K,ℓchat)=LLM⁡(𝐳,{𝐖(k)}k=1K),\displaystyle\big(\mathbf{E}^{\mathrm{llm}}_{t},\{\mathbf{Q}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K},\ell_{\mathrm{chat}}\big)=\mathrm{LLM}\big(\mathbf{z},\{\mathbf{W}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K}\big), (19)

where 𝐄tllm\mathbf{E}^{\mathrm{llm}}_{t} is a refined current BEV embedding and 𝐐(k)\mathbf{Q}^{(k)} are future-aware latent queries returned by the LLM; ℓchat\ell_{\mathrm{chat}} is language output. Analogous to the HERMES, the language output is designed to articulate responses to user queries regarding the driving environment, specifically encompassing scene descriptions and answers to visually-derived questions.The language supervision and world supervision interact enhanced with each other and unifies the world understanding and future scene generation. We then synthesize per-future-step BEV embeddings, followed by ego-attention refinement with 𝐖(k)\mathbf{W}^{(k)}:

𝐄~t+k↓\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}^{\downarrow}_{t+k} =𝐄tllm+𝐟frame​(k),\displaystyle=\mathbf{E}^{\mathrm{llm}}_{t}+\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{frame}}(k), (20)
𝐄t+k↓\displaystyle\mathbf{E}^{\downarrow}_{t+k} =EgoAttn(𝐄~t+k↓,𝐖(k)),k=1,…,K.\displaystyle=\mathrm{EgoAttn}\big(\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}^{\downarrow}_{t+k},~\mathbf{W}^{(k)}\big),k=1,\ldots,K. (21)

For completeness, the current-step BEV is given by 𝐳=𝐄tllm\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{E}^{\mathrm{llm}}_{t}.

B.3 Lifting BEV to 3D Voxel Features

Each 𝐄t+k↓\mathbf{E}^{\downarrow}_{t+k} is lifted to a 3D voxel representation via a depth-aware BEV upsampler:

𝐕t+k\displaystyle\mathbf{V}_{t+k} =BEVUpsample⁡(𝐄t+k↓)∈ℝC×Z×Hbev×Wbev,\displaystyle=\mathrm{BEVUpsample}\!\left(\mathbf{E}^{\downarrow}_{t+k}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times Z\times H_{\mathrm{bev}}\times W_{\mathrm{bev}}}, (22)
𝐔t+k\displaystyle\mathbf{U}_{t+k} =Conv3D⁡(𝐕t+k)∈ℝCout×Z×Hbev×Wbev,\displaystyle=\mathrm{Conv3D}\!\left(\mathbf{V}_{t+k}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{C_{\mathrm{out}}\times Z\times H_{\mathrm{bev}}\times W_{\mathrm{bev}}}, (23)

where BEVUpsample\mathrm{BEVUpsample} is a shallow 3D convolutions that reshapes the channel dimension into the vertical bins and upsamples from Z/2Z/2 to ZZ. 𝐔t+k\mathbf{U}_{t+k} is the unified 3D feature volume used for volumetric rendering.

B.4 LiDAR Ray Sampling and SDF-based Rendering

To recover fine-grained 3D geometry for each future frame t+kt+k, we follow the LiDAR acquisition process and construct a set of rays from the target point cloud Pt+kP_{t+k}. For each point 𝐱n∈Pt+k\mathbf{x}_{n}\in P_{t+k}, we define a ray originating from the sensor center and passing through the point. Formally, we sample

B.5 LiDAR Ray Sampling and SDF-based Rendering

We construct LiDAR rays for each future frame t+kt+k from the target point cloud Pt+kP_{t+k}. Each point 𝐱n∈Pt+k\mathbf{x}_{n}\in P_{t+k} defines one ray:

ℛt+k={(𝐨n,𝐝n,rn)}n=1N.\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{t+k}=\{(\mathbf{o}_{n},\mathbf{d}_{n},r_{n})\}_{n=1}^{N}. (24)

Here, 𝐨n\mathbf{o}_{n} is the ray origin in the LiDAR coordinate frame:

𝐨n=𝟎.\displaystyle\mathbf{o}_{n}=\mathbf{0}. (25)

This sets the origin of every ray to the sensor center, consistent with the LiDAR emission model.

The ray direction 𝐝n\mathbf{d}_{n} is computed by normalizing the vector from the origin to the observed point:

𝐝n=𝐱n−𝐨n‖𝐱n−𝐨n‖2.\displaystyle\mathbf{d}_{n}=\frac{\mathbf{x}_{n}-\mathbf{o}_{n}}{\|\mathbf{x}_{n}-\mathbf{o}_{n}\|_{2}}. (26)

This yields a unit-length direction pointing from the LiDAR toward 𝐱n\mathbf{x}_{n}.

The raw LiDAR range rnr_{n} is the Euclidean distance to the point:

rn=‖𝐱n−𝐨n‖2.\displaystyle r_{n}=\|\mathbf{x}_{n}-\mathbf{o}_{n}\|_{2}. (27)

We apply range filtering rmin<rn<rmaxr_{\min}<r_{n}<r_{\max} and optionally mask the ego-vehicle region to remove invalid measurements.

Ray-based SDF Rendering. Given the unified volumetric representation 𝐔t+k\mathbf{U}_{t+k}, we discretize each ray into nn sampled points:

𝐩i=𝐨n+di𝐝n,i=1,…,n,\displaystyle\mathbf{p}_{i}=\mathbf{o}_{n}+d_{i}\mathbf{d}_{n},\qquad i=1,\dots,n, (28)

where did_{i} denotes the sampled distance along the ray. For each 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i}, we retrieve its feature embedding 𝐟i\mathbf{f}_{i} from 𝐔t+k\mathbf{U}_{t+k} using trilinear interpolation.

A shallow MLP ϕSDF\phi_{\text{SDF}} predicts the signed distance value:

si=ϕSDF​(𝐩i,𝐟i).\displaystyle s_{i}=\phi_{\text{SDF}}(\mathbf{p}_{i},\mathbf{f}_{i}). (29)

Following volumetric SDF rendering, the opacity at the ii-th sample is computed as

αi=max⁡(σt​(si)−σt​(si+1)σt​(si), 0),σt​(x)=(1+e−t​x)−1,\displaystyle\alpha_{i}=\max\left(\frac{\sigma_{t}(s_{i})-\sigma_{t}(s_{i+1})}{\sigma_{t}(s_{i})},\,0\right),\sigma_{t}(x)=(1+e^{-tx})^{-1}, (30)

where σt​(⋅)\sigma_{t}(\cdot) is a learnable sigmoid modulation with parameter tt.

The accumulated transmittance TiT_{i} and the unbiased, occlusion-aware weight wiw_{i} follow:

Ti\displaystyle T_{i} =∏j=1i−1(1−αj),\displaystyle=\prod_{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\alpha_{j}), (31)
wi\displaystyle w_{i} =Ti​αi.\displaystyle=T_{i}\,\alpha_{i}. (32)

The rendered depth for ray (𝐨n,𝐝n)(\mathbf{o}_{n},\mathbf{d}_{n}) is then obtained via weighted integration:

r^n(k)=∑i=1nwi​di.\displaystyle\widehat{r}_{n}^{(k)}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\,d_{i}. (33)

Finally, the 3D point reconstructed by the renderer is

𝐱^n(k)=𝐨n+r^n(k)​𝐝n.\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{n}^{(k)}=\mathbf{o}_{n}+\widehat{r}_{n}^{(k)}\mathbf{d}_{n}. (34)

A global scale factor ss is applied consistently to all ray directions, sampled distances, and predicted depths to align the renderer’s internal metric space with real-world LiDAR geometry.

B.6 The pretrained Stage Training Objectives

During the pretraining stage, we supervise rendered depth and point clouds using per-ray regression and set-level geometry consistency. Let 𝒳(k)={𝐱n(k)}n=1N\mathcal{X}^{(k)}=\{\mathbf{x}_{n}^{(k)}\}_{n=1}^{N} and 𝒳^(k)={𝐱^n(k)}n=1N\widehat{\mathcal{X}}^{(k)}=\{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}_{n}^{(k)}\}_{n=1}^{N} be the ground-truth and predicted point sets:

ℒdepth\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{depth}} =1K​N​∑k=1K∑n=1N|rn−r^n(k)|,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{KN}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\big|\,r_{n}-\widehat{r}_{n}^{(k)}\,\big|, (35)
ℒchamfer\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{chamfer}} =1K∑k=1K[1|𝒳^(k)|∑𝐱^∈𝒳^(k)min𝐱∈𝒳(k)∥𝐱^−𝐱∥22\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Bigg[\frac{1}{|\widehat{\mathcal{X}}^{(k)}|}\sum_{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}\in\widehat{\mathcal{X}}^{(k)}}\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}^{(k)}}\|\widehat{\mathbf{x}}-\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}
+1|𝒳(k)|∑𝐱∈𝒳(k)min𝐱^∈𝒳^(k)∥𝐱−𝐱^∥22].\displaystyle+\frac{1}{|\mathcal{X}^{(k)}|}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}^{(k)}}\min_{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}\in\widehat{\mathcal{X}}^{(k)}}\|\mathbf{x}-\widehat{\mathbf{x}}\|_{2}^{2}\Bigg].

The renderer also returns auxiliary losses ℒrender\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{render}} (e.g., density/color regularizers). When conversational pretraining is enabled, an LLM supervision ℒchat\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{chat}} is added. The full objective is

ℒ=λrender​ℒrender+λdepth​ℒdepth\displaystyle\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{\mathrm{render}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{render}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{depth}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{depth}} (36)
+λch​ℒchamfer+λchat​ℒchat.\displaystyle+\lambda_{\mathrm{ch}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{chamfer}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{chat}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{chat}}. (37)

B.7 Implementation Details

We use half-precision for BEV tensors entering the LLM and enable gradient checkpointing for the LLM, BEV upsampler, and rendering convolutions to reduce memory. The ego-attention in DownSampleCross\mathrm{DownSampleCross} is activated only when Nq>0N_{q}>0, allowing the LLM’s future-aware queries to modulate per-future BEV embeddings. All per-frame volumes share the same renderer fθf_{\theta} and voxelization parameters to ensure temporal consistency.

C Comparison between Different MoE

Preliminaries.

Let xb,t∈ℝdx_{b,t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be the tt-th token in the bb-th sample, and let each expert FFN with parameters {W1(e)∈ℝd×m,W3(e)∈ℝd×m,W2(e)∈ℝm×d}\{W_{1}^{(e)}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{d\times m},\,W_{3}^{(e)}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{d\times m},\,W_{2}^{(e)}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}\}. Define the nominal FFN cost Cffn≈(2​d​m+m​d)C_{\text{ffn}}\approx(2dm+md) FLOPs per token.

C.1 SparseMoE (Top-kk Token Routing)

Sparse MoE routes each token independently to a small subset of experts. Let pb,t∈ΔE−1p_{b,t}\in\Delta^{E-1} be the gate over experts and 𝒯k​(b,t)\mathcal{T}_{k}(b,t) the top-kk indices. The layer output is

yb,tsparse=∑e∈𝒯k​(b,t)pb,t,e​f(e)​(xb,t).y_{b,t}^{\text{sparse}}=\!\!\sum_{e\in\mathcal{T}_{k}(b,t)}\!\!p_{b,t,e}\,f^{(e)}(x_{b,t}).

Routing is token-level, irregular, and requires dispatch/gather. Complexity is 𝒪⁡(B​L​k​Cffn)\mathcal{O}(BLk\,C_{\text{ffn}}) per layer (sequence length LL), with additional routing overhead and potential load imbalance. Auxiliary balancing losses are commonly required.

C.2 SoftMoE (Slot Aggregation Without Top-kk)

Soft Mixture-of-Experts replaces hard top-kk routing with continuous token-to-expert assignment. Each expert contains learnable slots S∈ℝE×S×dS\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times S\times d}, and token–slot affinities are computed by

lb,t,e,s=⟨xb,t,Se,s⟩.\displaystyle l_{b,t,e,s}=\langle x_{b,t},\,S_{e,s}\rangle. (38)

A softmax over (e,s)(e,s) dispatches each token fractionally to all expert slots, which are then aggregated before passing through the expert FFN. This avoids load imbalance and exercises all experts every step, but incurs full expert computation, resulting in

𝒪⁡(B​E​S​Cffn),\displaystyle\mathcal{O}(BES\,C_{\text{ffn}}), (39)

and increased memory due to slot embeddings.

C.3 SA-MoE

We introduce a sample-level, BEV-conditioned, weight-merging MoE that avoids token dispatch and executes a single FFN while preserving expert specialization. SA-MoE runs a single FFN per token: 𝒪⁡(B​L​Cffn)\mathcal{O}(BL\,C_{\text{ffn}}), plus a per-sample merge cost 𝒪⁡(E⁡(d​m+m​d))\mathcal{O}\big(E(dm+md)\big) to form W^i(b)\hat{W}_{i}^{(b)} (independent of LL and small for moderate EE). Compared with SparseMoE, SA-MoE removes token dispatch, padding/gather, and imbalance. Compared with SoftMoE, it avoids the all-expert forward and slot memory.

C.4 Qualitative Comparison

  • •

    Routing signal. SparseMoE routes by token content; SoftMoE routes by token-to-slot similarity; SA-MoE routes by BEV-derived scene cues.

  • •

    Routing granularity. SparseMoE: token-level; SoftMoE: token-to-slot; SA-MoE: sample-level.

  • •

    Mixture locus. Sparse/Soft: mix outputs in activation space; SA-MoE: mix parameters to synthesize a sample-specific FFN.

  • •

    Efficiency. SparseMoE: ∝k\propto k experts per token + dispatch overhead; SoftMoE: all experts each step; SA-MoE: one FFN per token + cheap merges, highly GPU-friendly.

  • •

    Specialization and stability. SparseMoE encourages sharp specialization but needs balancing. SoftMoE is stable but compute-heavy. SA-MoE inherits stability (softmax over experts) and yields coherent sample-level specialization via BEV cues, while keeping cost close to dense FFN.

D Additional Experiment Details

D.1 Additional Details Training Stages

Our framework is trained in two main stages, with pretraining stage consisting of three sequential steps that establish multimodal perception and world modeling followed HERMES[52].

Step 1: BEVEncoder Pretraining. The BEV encoder EE and point cloud render RR are trained to map input images ItI_{t} into point clouds via Pt=R⁡(E⁡(It))P_{t}=R(E(I_{t})), using 12Hz data from the nuScenes training set.

Step 2: BEV-Text Alignment and Refinement. Vision-language alignment is established through in-projections for flattened BEV embeddings and out-projections for encoded BEV features, trained on NuInteract dense captions. To alleviate data scarcity, a masking-based augmentation is applied: one multi-view image is masked, and its caption is spliced from visible views, yielding approximately 200K image-text pairs—seven times the original nuScenes keyframe set. Subsequently, all parameters are unfrozen and the LLM is fine-tuned using LoRA, with supervision from scene descriptions in OmniDrive-nuScenes.

Step 3: Understanding and Generation Unification. Future point cloud generation modules are introduced and trained jointly with existing components using nuScenes keyframes, scene descriptions, and general conversation annotations from OmniDrive-nuScenes.

In the pretraining stage, the planning expert is frozen while the world-language expert is trained with a combined objective: language modeling loss for scene understanding and point cloud reconstruction loss for world prediction. Flow-matching loss ℒflow​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{flow}}(\theta) guides action interpolation toward true trajectories using multimodal context 𝒞\mathcal{C} (BEV tokens, language, world state, ego-motion), enabling smooth, context-aware forecasting.

The final stage has two phases: (1) train without MoE for stability, then (2) initialize the soft-weighted MoE sub-experts in the planning expert directly from the learned weights, enabling expert specialization while preserving pretraining knowledge.

D.2 Additional Details About Comparison to Existing MoE Mechanism

We further present the numerical results of different MoE implementation in Table 4. To isolate the contribution of Scene Adaptive MoE, we construct two ablation baselines with BEV bais. We present the details of these baseline,

SoftMoE w/ BEV Bias. We extend the standard soft mixture-of-experts architecture by injecting BEV features into the slot-based routing mechanism. Each expert is associated with learnable slot embeddings S∈ℝE×S×dS\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times S\times d}, and given token features x∈ℝB×N×dx\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times N\times d} and BEV features hbevh_{\mathrm{bev}}, the routing logits are computed as

logits=⟨x,S⟩⋅ωslot+(⟨HBEV,S⟩⊙α)⋅ωbev,\mathrm{logits}=\langle x,S\rangle\cdot\omega_{\mathrm{slot}}\;+\;\big(\langle H_{\mathrm{BEV}},S\rangle\odot\alpha\big)\cdot\omega_{\mathrm{bev}}, (40)

where α∈ℝE\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{E} is a learnable per-expert scaling factor. The dispatch weights are obtained by normalizing logits across tokens and slots. Each expert processes its assigned slot representation using

MLP⁡(x)=W2​(σ⁡(W1​x)⊙W3​x).\mathrm{MLP}(x)=W_{2}\!\left(\sigma(W_{1}x)\odot W_{3}x\right). (41)

This baseline evaluates whether BEV-conditioned slot affinity improves soft expert merging.

SparseMoE w/ BEV-Aware Gating. We further build a sparse MoE variant where BEV features directly bias the top-kk gating function. The routing logits are computed as

router​_​logits=ωtok​Wtok​x+ωbev​Wbev​HBEV,\mathrm{router\_logits}=\omega_{\mathrm{tok}}\,W_{\mathrm{tok}}x+\omega_{\mathrm{bev}}\,W_{\mathrm{bev}}H_{\mathrm{BEV}}, (42)

followed by a softmax and top-kk selection per token. The selected routing probabilities are renormalized, and each active expert processes only its assigned tokens:

ExpertOutpute​(x)=MLPe​(x)⋅pe​(x).\mathrm{ExpertOutput}_{e}(x)=\mathrm{MLP}_{e}(x)\cdot p_{e}(x). (43)

The outputs from all activated experts are accumulated to obtain the final hidden representation.These two baselines allow us to disentangle the respective effects of BEV-aware soft slot routing and BEV-biased sparse top-kk gating.

E Theoretical Analysis of SAMoE

In this section we provide a theoretical analysis and formal justification on the representation capacity, temporal causality stability, convergence advantages, and gradient stability of SAMoE.

E.1 Preliminaries

Scene-Optimal Parameter and Its Decomposition

For a specific model parameter vector θ\theta, the flow-matching loss is defined as follows:

Lflow​(θ)=𝔼x0,t,ϵ|s​‖vθ​(xt,t)−v∗​(xt,t)‖2L_{\mathrm{flow}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},\,t,\,\epsilon\mid s}\left\|v_{\theta}(x_{t},t)-v^{*}(x_{t},t)\right\|^{2} (44)

Each scene is denoted by ss, and represented by a bird’s-eye-view feature map HBEVH_{\mathrm{BEV}}. We define a scene-conditional optimum parameter vector θ∗​(s)\theta^{*}(s) as

θ∗​(s)=arg⁡minθ​𝔼x0,t,ϵ|s​‖vθ​(xt,t)−v∗​(xt,t)‖2,\theta^{*}(s)=\arg\min_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},\,t,\,\epsilon\mid s}\left\|v_{\theta}(x_{t},t)-v^{*}(x_{t},t)\right\|^{2}, (45)

where the conditional expectation is restricted to data belonging to scene ss. Thus θ∗​(s)\theta^{*}(s) is the parameter vector that minimizes the flow-matching loss for that specific scene.

We only require the existence of at least one measurable selection of scene-optimal parameters θ∗​(s)\theta^{*}(s). uniqueness is not needed, and all results hold for any such selection.

Mild Representability Assumption for Experts

We consider a mixture-of-experts architecture with EE experts {F(e)}e=1E\{F^{(e)}\}_{e=1}^{E}, where each expert ee is parameterized by weight matrices {Wi(e)}i=1M\{W_{i}^{(e)}\}_{i=1}^{M} and has full parameter vector θ(e)\theta^{(e)}.

Approximate scene-wise linearization.

Rather than assuming the experts’ convex hull strictly contains the scene-optimal parameters, we adopt a mild representability condition: for each scene ss, there exist mixture weights π∗​(s)∈ΔE−1\pi^{*}(s)\in\Delta^{E-1} such that the resulting linear combination

Θ⁡(π∗​(s)):=∑e=1Eπe∗​(s)​θ(e)\Theta(\pi^{*}(s)):=\sum_{e=1}^{E}\pi_{e}^{*}(s)\,\theta^{(e)} (46)

provides a reasonable local linear approximation to the scene-optimal parameter θ∗​(s)\theta^{*}(s):

‖θ∗​(s)−Θ⁡(π∗​(s))‖≤ϵs,\|\theta^{*}(s)-\Theta(\pi^{*}(s))\|\leq\epsilon_{s}, (47)

for some small ϵs\epsilon_{s} depending on scene ss.

Justification.

This condition is sufficient but not necessary for our theoretical analysis. It can be motivated by the following observations:

  1. 1.

    Joint MoE training encourages experts to specialize in different regions of the scene distribution.

  2. 2.

    Smoothness and parameter sharing imply that scene-optimal parameters vary on a low-curvature manifold.

  3. 3.

    By standard first-order Taylor or RCT-based arguments, any sufficiently smooth function over a low-curvature manifold can be locally approximated by a linear combination of nearby points (experts).

Lemma (local linear approximation).

Suppose the scene-optimal parameter manifold has local curvature bounded by CC and the set of experts {θ(e)}\{\theta^{(e)}\} covers the scene space with distance at most δ\delta. Then for any scene ss, there exists a convex combination of experts Θ​(π∗​(s))\Theta(\pi^{*}(s)) such that

‖θ∗​(s)−Θ⁡(π∗​(s))‖≤C​δ2.\|\theta^{*}(s)-\Theta(\pi^{*}(s))\|\leq C\delta^{2}. (48)

This formalizes the sense in which experts can provide a local linear approximation to θ∗​(s)\theta^{*}(s) without assuming exact convex-span representability.

Two-sided (bi-Lipschitz) bounds on the model map.

We now state and prove the two-sided Lipschitz-type inequalities we will use repeatedly in the sequel. Fix a data point (x,t)(x,t) and consider the model map θ↦vθ​(x,t)∈ℝd\theta\mapsto v_{\theta}(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Assumption A (Upper Lipschitz).

There exists a constant L>0L>0 such that for all admissible parameters θ,θ′\theta,\theta^{\prime},

‖vθ​(x,t)−vθ′​(x,t)‖2≤L​‖θ−θ′‖2.\|v_{\theta}(x,t)-v_{\theta^{\prime}}(x,t)\|_{2}\leq L\,\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|_{2}. (49)

This is the standard Lipschitz continuity assumption on the parameter map. In modern neural architectures this assumption is mild: each expert is composed of affine layers and Lipschitz activation functions (e.g., ReLU, GeLU), so the overall map θ↦vθ\theta\mapsto v_{\theta} is itself Lipschitz with a constant determined by the product of layer-wise spectral norms. Moreover, common training practices such as weight decay, LayerNorm, residual connections, and gradient clipping implicitly control the operator norms of intermediate layers, ensuring that the global Lipschitz constant LL remains finite throughout training.

Assumption B (Local Bi-Lipschitz / Mild Non-degeneracy).

We assume that the model map θ↦vθ​(x,t)\theta\mapsto v_{\theta}(x,t) is continuously differentiable and satisfies a local Jacobian lower bound along the regions of parameter space actually traversed by mixture combinations during training:

Jθ​(x,t)⊤​Jθ​(x,t)⪰λ2​I,∀θ∈conv⁡({θ(e)}e=1E)∩ℛtrain,J_{\theta}(x,t)^{\top}J_{\theta}(x,t)\succeq\lambda^{2}I,\qquad\forall\theta\in\mathrm{conv}\bigl(\{\theta^{(e)}\}_{e=1}^{E}\bigr)\cap\mathcal{R}_{\text{train}}, (50)

where ℛtrain\mathcal{R}_{\text{train}} denotes the low-dimensional subspace of parameters explored by the mixture weights during training.

Equivalently, the Jacobian has singular values at least λ\lambda almost everywhere in the relevant region of parameter space. This mild local curvature assumption ensures that perturbations in the mixture weights induce nontrivial changes in the model output, without requiring the model to be globally injective or globally bi-Lipschitz.

Claim.

Under Assumptions A and B (local non-degeneracy along the training-relevant region), there exist constants L≥c>0L\geq c>0 (with c=λc=\lambda) such that for all θ,θ′∈conv⁡({θ(e)}e=1E)∩ℛtrain\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\mathrm{conv}\bigl(\{\theta^{(e)}\}_{e=1}^{E}\bigr)\cap\mathcal{R}_{\text{train}},

c​‖θ−θ′‖2≤‖vθ​(x,t)−vθ′​(x,t)‖2≤L​‖θ−θ′‖2.c\,\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|_{2}\leq\|v_{\theta}(x,t)-v_{\theta^{\prime}}(x,t)\|_{2}\leq L\,\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|_{2}. (51)
Proof.

The upper bound is exactly (49) and holds globally.

For the lower bound, assume θ,θ′∈conv⁡({θ(e)}e=1E)∩ℛtrain\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\mathrm{conv}\bigl(\{\theta^{(e)}\}_{e=1}^{E}\bigr)\cap\mathcal{R}_{\text{train}} and set Δ​θ:=θ−θ′\Delta\theta:=\theta-\theta^{\prime}. Consider the line segment γ⁡(u)=θ′+u​Δ​θ\gamma(u)=\theta^{\prime}+u\Delta\theta, u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1], which lies entirely within the convex hull of expert parameters and the training-relevant region. By the fundamental theorem of calculus (vector-valued mean value / integral form)

vθ​(x,t)−vθ′​(x,t)=∫01Jγ⁡(u)​(x,t)​𝑑u​Δ​θ.v_{\theta}(x,t)-v_{\theta^{\prime}}(x,t)=\int_{0}^{1}J_{\gamma(u)}(x,t)\,du\;\;\Delta\theta. (52)

Using the local Jacobian lower bound along this segment,

‖vθ−vθ′‖22\displaystyle\|v_{\theta}-v_{\theta^{\prime}}\|_{2}^{2} =Δ​θ⊤​(∫01Jγ⁡(u)⊤​Jγ⁡(u)​𝑑u)​Δ​θ\displaystyle=\Delta\theta^{\top}\Big(\int_{0}^{1}J_{\gamma(u)}^{\top}J_{\gamma(u)}\,du\Big)\Delta\theta
≥λ2​‖Δ​θ‖22,\displaystyle\geq\lambda^{2}\|\Delta\theta\|_{2}^{2}, (53)

where λ\lambda is the minimal singular value of JθJ_{\theta} in the training-relevant convex hull. Taking the square root yields the desired lower bound c=λc=\lambda.

∎

Conclusion.

Under Assumptions A and B (local non-degeneracy), the model map θ↦vθ​(x,t)\theta\mapsto v_{\theta}(x,t) satisfies the two-sided (bi-Lipschitz) inequalities

c​‖θ−θ′‖2≤‖vθ​(x,t)−vθ′​(x,t)‖2≤L​‖θ−θ′‖2,\displaystyle c\,\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|_{2}\leq\|v_{\theta}(x,t)-v_{\theta^{\prime}}(x,t)\|_{2}\leq L\,\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|_{2},
∀θ,θ′∈conv⁡({θ(e)}e=1E)∩ℛtrain,\displaystyle\quad\forall\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\mathrm{conv}\bigl(\{\theta^{(e)}\}_{e=1}^{E}\bigr)\cap\mathcal{R}_{\text{train}}, (54)

with constants LL (global Lipschitz) and cc (local Jacobian lower bound). The upper bound LL controls the maximum sensitivity of the output to parameter changes globally, while the lower bound cc ensures nontrivial output variation along convex combinations of expert parameters in the training-relevant region, without requiring full global injectivity in the entire parameter space.

Representation Capacity Theory of SAMoE

We analyze how a parameter-level soft merge approximates convex combinations of expert outputs, and we derive a quantitative bound on the nonlinear residual introduced by merging inside the parameters. This subsection provides a compact form of the representation-capacity result used later to compare SAMoE with token-level MoE and dense baselines.

Setup.

Each expert e∈{1,…,E}e\in\{1,\dots,E\} contains parameters {W1(e),W2(e),W3(e)}\{W^{(e)}_{1},W^{(e)}_{2},W^{(e)}_{3}\}. Given mixture weights π∈ΔE−1\pi\in\Delta^{E-1}, the merged layer uses the convexly combined parameters

Wi​(π)=∑e=1Eπe​Wi(e).W_{i}(\pi)=\sum_{e=1}^{E}\pi_{e}W_{i}^{(e)}. (55)

The nonlinear layer considered throughout the paper is

FW​(x)=σ⁡(x​W1)⊙(x​W3)​W2,F_{W}(x)=\sigma(xW_{1})\odot(xW_{3})\,W_{2}, (56)

with elementwise nonlinearity σ\sigma.

We assume: (i) σ\sigma is twice differentiable with bounded first and second derivatives; (ii) input features satisfy ‖x‖2≤Bx\|x\|_{2}\leq B_{x}; (iii) all expert weight matrices are bounded by ‖Wi(e)‖F≤BW\|W_{i}^{(e)}\|_{F}\leq B_{W}. These are standard smoothness and boundedness assumptions for modern deep layers.

Linear case: exact convexity.

If the layer is linear, f(e)​(x)=x​W(e)f^{(e)}(x)=xW^{(e)}, then for any π\pi,

x​W​(π)=∑eπe​x​W(e).xW(\pi)=\sum_{e}\pi_{e}\,xW^{(e)}. (57)

Thus parameter-level merging is exactly equivalent to output-level mixing. Linear layers therefore incur no representation gap.

Nonlinear case: defining the residual.

Define the nonlinear merging error as

Δπ​(x)=FW⁡(π)​(x)−∑eπe​FW(e)​(x).\Delta_{\pi}(x)=F_{W(\pi)}(x)-\sum_{e}\pi_{e}F_{W^{(e)}}(x). (58)

This term is zero for linear layers, and also zero for one-hot π\pi, but nonzero in general due to the nonlinearity in (56).

Representation–capacity bound.

We show that the nonlinear residual is controlled by the pairwise dispersion of experts:

‖Δπ​(x)‖2≤C​∑e≠e′πe​πe′​‖W(e)−W(e′)‖F2,\|\Delta_{\pi}(x)\|_{2}\;\leq\;C\sum_{e\neq e^{\prime}}\pi_{e}\pi_{e^{\prime}}\|W^{(e)}-W^{(e^{\prime})}\|_{F}^{2}, (59)

for a constant CC depending only on the layer dimensions, activation curvature, and bounds on xx and {W(e)}\{W^{(e)}\}. When experts are similar or π\pi is sparse, the right-hand side vanishes, recovering the exact convex representation.

Proof (Sketch of Proof)

Let g⁡(W)=σ⁡(x​W)g(W)=\sigma(xW) denote the nonlinear layer with a smooth activation σ\sigma. Since σ\sigma has bounded second derivative, gg is twice differentiable with Hessian norm uniformly bounded by a constant HσH_{\sigma} depending only on the activation curvature and ‖x‖\|x\|.

Consider the convex combination W⁡(π)=∑eπe​W(e)W(\pi)=\sum_{e}\pi_{e}W^{(e)}. A second-order Taylor expansion of g⁡(W(e))g(W^{(e)}) around W⁡(π)W(\pi) yields

g⁡(W(e))=g⁡(W⁡(π))+⟨∇g​(W⁡(π)),W(e)−W⁡(π)⟩+Re,g(W^{(e)})\;=\;g(W(\pi))\;+\;\langle\nabla g(W(\pi)),\,W^{(e)}-W(\pi)\rangle\;+\;R_{e}, (60)

where the remainder satisfies

‖Re‖≤C0​‖W(e)−W⁡(π)‖F2\|R_{e}\|\;\leq\;C_{0}\,\|W^{(e)}-W(\pi)\|_{F}^{2} (61)

for some constant C0C_{0} depending only on HσH_{\sigma} and the layer dimensions.

Using ∑eπe​(W(e)−W⁡(π))=0\sum_{e}\pi_{e}(W^{(e)}-W(\pi))=0, the linear terms cancel when we form the mixture ∑eπe​g​(W(e))\sum_{e}\pi_{e}g(W^{(e)}), giving

Δπ(x)=g(W(π))−∑eπeg(W(e))=−∑eπeRe.\Delta_{\pi}(x)=g(W(\pi))-\sum_{e}\pi_{e}g(W^{(e)})=-\sum_{e}\pi_{e}R_{e}. (62)

Taking norms and substituting the bound on ReR_{e},

‖Δπ​(x)‖≤C0​∑eπe​‖W(e)−W⁡(π)‖F2.\|\Delta_{\pi}(x)\|\;\leq\;C_{0}\sum_{e}\pi_{e}\|W^{(e)}-W(\pi)\|_{F}^{2}. (63)

Finally, expanding around the mean shows that

∑eπe​‖W(e)−W⁡(π)‖F2=12​∑e≠e′πe​πe′​‖W(e)−W(e′)‖F2,\sum_{e}\pi_{e}\|W^{(e)}-W(\pi)\|_{F}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{e\neq e^{\prime}}\pi_{e}\pi_{e^{\prime}}\|W^{(e)}-W^{(e^{\prime})}\|_{F}^{2}, (64)

which completes the proof after absorbing constants.

Interpretation.

The decomposition

FW⁡(π)​(x)=∑eπe​FW(e)​(x)⏟ideal convex combination+Δπ​(x)⏟nonlinear residualF_{W(\pi)}(x)=\underbrace{\sum_{e}\pi_{e}F_{W^{(e)}}(x)}_{\text{ideal convex combination}}\;+\;\underbrace{\Delta_{\pi}(x)}_{\text{nonlinear residual}} (65)

shows that the residual is small whenever: (1) experts lie close together in parameter space, or (2) π\pi is sparse (top-11 / top-kk routing), or (3) the merged point W⁡(π)W(\pi) lies near a low-variance region of the expert set.

This representation-capacity analysis provides the foundation for the comparisons of token-level MoE and SAMoE, where token-level MoE and dense baselines are shown to incur irreducible error when their routing weights cannot match the scene-optimal mixture.

Fundamental Limitation of Token-Level Routing Under Local Information

We analyze the expressive limitation of token-level MoE routing under restricted information access.

Scene-Optimal Mixture.

For each scene ss, let

π∗​(s)∈ΔE−1\pi^{*}(s)\in\Delta^{E-1} (66)

denote the scene-optimal expert mixture, and define

θ∗​(s)=∑e=1Eπe∗​(s)​θ(e).\theta^{*}(s)=\sum_{e=1}^{E}\pi_{e}^{*}(s)\,\theta^{(e)}. (67)

We assume:

  1. 1.

    π∗​(s)\pi^{*}(s) lies in the interior of the simplex with non-zero probability;

  2. 2.

    π∗​(s)\pi^{*}(s) depends on global scene attributes.

Assumption (Local Routing).

The router of token-level MoE receives only a single token embedding xt(i)x_{t}^{(i)} and does not access global scene features, BEV summaries, or long-range context.

Thus routing is of the form

π(i)=Router⁡(xt(i)).\pi^{(i)}=\mathrm{Router}(x_{t}^{(i)}). (68)

Let 𝒢local\mathcal{G}_{\text{local}} denote the class of routing functions measurable with respect to local token information.

Local-Information Lower Bound.

Define the best achievable routing under local information:

πbest(i)=arg⁡minπ∈𝒢local​‖π−π∗​(s)‖.\pi^{(i)}_{\text{best}}=\arg\min_{\pi\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{local}}}\|\pi-\pi^{*}(s)\|. (69)

Since π∗​(s)\pi^{*}(s) depends on global scene attributes not observable from xt(i)x_{t}^{(i)}, the approximation error is strictly positive:

infπ∈𝒢local‖π−π∗​(s)‖≥εlocal​(s)>0.\inf_{\pi\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{local}}}\|\pi-\pi^{*}(s)\|\geq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{local}}(s)>0. (70)

This lower bound holds whenever scene-level variables influencing π∗​(s)\pi^{*}(s) are conditionally independent of xt(i)x_{t}^{(i)}.

Top-kk Sparsification Constraint.

Sparse token-level MoE further restricts routing to

Sπ(i)=Top​-​k​(π(i)),|Sπ(i)|=k,S_{\pi^{(i)}}=\mathrm{Top}\text{-}k(\pi^{(i)}),\qquad|S_{\pi^{(i)}}|=k, (71)

so that

πe(i)=0for ​e∉Sπ(i).\pi_{e}^{(i)}=0\quad\text{for }e\notin S_{\pi^{(i)}}. (72)

Let

𝒮k=⋃|S|=kconv⁡({𝐞e:e∈S})\mathcal{S}_{k}=\bigcup_{|S|=k}\mathrm{conv}\big(\{\mathbf{e}_{e}:e\in S\}\big) (73)

denote the union of all kk-dimensional faces of the simplex.

If π∗​(s)\pi^{*}(s) lies in the interior of ΔE−1\Delta^{E-1}, then

infπ∈𝒮k‖π−π∗​(s)‖≥εtopk​(s)>0.\inf_{\pi\in\mathcal{S}_{k}}\|\pi-\pi^{*}(s)\|\geq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{topk}}(s)>0. (74)

This reflects the geometric fact that interior points cannot be exactly represented by mixtures supported on only k<Ek<E experts.

Unified Approximation Gap.

Combining (70) and (74), any routing satisfying both local-information and top-kk constraints obeys

‖π(i)−π∗​(s)‖≥εtk​(s):=εlocal​(s)+εtopk​(s)>0.\|\pi^{(i)}-\pi^{*}(s)\|\geq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tk}}(s):=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{local}}(s)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{topk}}(s)>0. (75)
Proposition 1 (Token-Level Routing Gap)

Under local routing, the minimal deviation from the scene-optimal mixture satisfies

infπ∈𝒢local‖π−π∗​(s)‖≥εlocal​(s)>0.\inf_{\pi\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{local}}}\|\pi-\pi^{*}(s)\|\geq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{local}}(s)>0. (76)

Under both local routing and top-kk sparsification,

infπ∈𝒢local∩𝒮k‖π−π∗​(s)‖≥εtopk​(s)>0.\inf_{\pi\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{local}}\cap\mathcal{S}_{k}}\|\pi-\pi^{*}(s)\|\geq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{topk}}(s)>0. (77)
Corollary 1 (Sparse Token-Level MoE).

Sparse MoE satisfies both constraints, hence incurs an irreducible mixture approximation gap εtopk​(s)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{topk}}(s).

Corollary 2 (Soft Token-Level MoE).

Soft MoE removes the top-kk constraint, so εtopk​(s)=0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{topk}}(s)=0. However, under local routing it still satisfies

infπ∈𝒢local‖π−π∗​(s)‖≥εlocal​(s)>0.\inf_{\pi\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{local}}}\|\pi-\pi^{*}(s)\|\geq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{local}}(s)>0. (78)

Thus Soft MoE reduces but does not eliminate the representation gap.

Implication.

The gap originates from an information granularity mismatch: token-level routing operates on local embeddings, whereas π∗​(s)\pi^{*}(s) depends on global scene-level attributes.

This mismatch directly leads to irreducible function approximation error in token-level MoE variants, which will be contrasted with the scene-level routing mechanism of SAMoE in the next subsection.

E.2 Comparison of Representation Capacity Across MoE Variants

We compare the expressive power of four architectures: (i) SAMoE (scene-level soft parameter merging), (ii) Dense networks, (iii) Sparse token-level MoE (top-kk routing), (iv) Soft token-level MoE.

Let π∗​(s)∈ΔE−1\pi^{*}(s)\in\Delta^{E-1} denote the scene-optimal expert mixture, and define the corresponding scene-optimal parameter

θ∗​(s)=∑e=1Eπe∗​(s)​θ(e).\theta^{*}(s)=\sum_{e=1}^{E}\pi_{e}^{*}(s)\,\theta^{(e)}. (79)

We assume θ∗​(s)\theta^{*}(s) varies across scenes with non-zero variance.

1. Representation Capacity of SAMoE

SAMoE produces scene-dependent parameters

θSAMoE​(s)=∑e=1Eπe​(s)​θ(e),\theta_{\text{SAMoE}}(s)=\sum_{e=1}^{E}\pi_{e}(s)\,\theta^{(e)}, (80)

where the router observes global scene features.

From the Representation Capacity Theory (RCT) derived earlier, the nonlinear merging residual satisfies

‖Δπ​(x)‖≤C​∑e≠e′πe​πe′​‖W(e)−W(e′)‖F2.\|\Delta_{\pi}(x)\|\leq C\sum_{e\neq e^{\prime}}\pi_{e}\pi_{e^{\prime}}\|W^{(e)}-W^{(e^{\prime})}\|_{F}^{2}. (81)

Assume the router approximates π∗​(s)\pi^{*}(s) up to error δ⁡(s)\delta(s):

‖π⁡(s)−π∗​(s)‖≤δ⁡(s).\|\pi(s)-\pi^{*}(s)\|\leq\delta(s). (82)

Then the approximation error satisfies

𝔼⁡[‖fθSAMoE​(s)​(x)−fθ∗​(s)​(x)‖2]≤O⁡(δ​(s)2)+O⁡(expert dispersion).\mathbb{E}\big[\|f_{\theta_{\text{SAMoE}}(s)}(x)-f_{\theta^{*}(s)}(x)\|^{2}\big]\leq O(\delta(s)^{2})+O(\text{expert dispersion}). (83)

If experts cover the parameter manifold and the router is consistent, this error can be made arbitrarily small:

inff∈ℱSAMoE𝔼​‖f⁡(x,s)−f∗​(x,s)‖=0.\inf_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{\text{SAMoE}}}\mathbb{E}\|f(x,s)-f^{*}(x,s)\|=0. (84)

Thus SAMoE can approximate the scene-optimal function arbitrarily well.

2. Representation Capacity of Dense Networks

A dense model uses a single shared parameter vector θD\theta_{D} independent of ss.

To represent all scenes perfectly, one would require

θD≈θ∗​(s)∀s.\theta_{D}\approx\theta^{*}(s)\quad\forall s. (85)

If θ∗​(s)\theta^{*}(s) varies across scenes, this condition is impossible.

Specifically, for two scenes s1,s2s_{1},s_{2} such that

‖θ∗​(s1)−θ∗​(s2)‖≥γ>0,\|\theta^{*}(s_{1})-\theta^{*}(s_{2})\|\geq\gamma>0, (86)

any shared parameter θD\theta_{D} satisfies

maxs∈{s1,s2}⁡‖θD−θ∗​(s)‖≥γ2.\max_{s\in\{s_{1},s_{2}\}}\|\theta_{D}-\theta^{*}(s)\|\geq\frac{\gamma}{2}. (87)

Therefore,

inff∈ℱDense𝔼​‖f⁡(x,s)−f∗​(x,s)‖≥c​γ.\inf_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{\text{Dense}}}\mathbb{E}\|f(x,s)-f^{*}(x,s)\|\geq c\gamma. (88)

Dense networks exhibit an irreducible representation gap.

3. Representation Capacity of Sparse Token-Level MoE

Sparse MoE performs token-level routing:

π(i)=Router⁡(x(i)),Sπ(i)=Top​-​k​(π(i)).\pi^{(i)}=\mathrm{Router}(x^{(i)}),\qquad S_{\pi^{(i)}}=\mathrm{Top}\text{-}k(\pi^{(i)}). (89)

Each token realizes parameters

θ(i)=∑e∈Sπ(i)πe(i)​θ(e).\theta^{(i)}=\sum_{e\in S_{\pi^{(i)}}}\pi_{e}^{(i)}\theta^{(e)}. (90)

This restricts feasible mixtures to a union of kk-dimensional faces of the simplex.

If π∗​(s)\pi^{*}(s) lies in the interior of ΔE−1\Delta^{E-1}, then

‖π(i)−π∗​(s)‖≥εtopk​(s)>0.\|\pi^{(i)}-\pi^{*}(s)\|\geq\varepsilon_{\text{topk}}(s)>0. (91)

Under the local-routing assumption (the router observes only token-level embeddings),

‖π(i)−π∗​(s)‖≥εlocal​(s)>0.\|\pi^{(i)}-\pi^{*}(s)\|\geq\varepsilon_{\text{local}}(s)>0. (92)

Combining both constraints,

‖π(i)−π∗​(s)‖≥εtk​(s)>0.\|\pi^{(i)}-\pi^{*}(s)\|\geq\varepsilon_{\text{tk}}(s)>0. (93)

Thus Sparse MoE incurs an irreducible representation gap:

inff∈ℱSparse𝔼​‖f⁡(x,s)−f∗​(x,s)‖≥c​εtk​(s).\inf_{f\in\mathcal{F}_{\text{Sparse}}}\mathbb{E}\|f(x,s)-f^{*}(x,s)\|\geq c\,\varepsilon_{\text{tk}}(s). (94)
