4. Representation Capacity of Soft Token-Level MoE

Soft MoE removes the top-kk constraint:

θ(i)=∑e=1Eπe(i)​θ(e).\theta^{(i)}=\sum_{e=1}^{E}\pi_{e}^{(i)}\theta^{(e)}. (95)

This eliminates εtopk​(s)\varepsilon_{\text{topk}}(s).

However, under the local-routing assumption, the router still lacks access to global scene information, so

‖π(i)−π∗​(s)‖≥εlocal​(s)>0.\|\pi^{(i)}-\pi^{*}(s)\|\geq\varepsilon_{\text{local}}(s)>0. (96)

Hence Soft MoE reduces but does not eliminate the representation gap.

5. Representation Hierarchy

Under the stated assumptions, the function classes satisfy

ℱDense⊊ℱSparse⊊ℱSoft⊊ℱSAMoE.\mathcal{F}_{\text{Dense}}\subsetneq\mathcal{F}_{\text{Sparse}}\subsetneq\mathcal{F}_{\text{Soft}}\subsetneq\mathcal{F}_{\text{SAMoE}}. (97)

The inclusions are strict whenever:

  • •

    scene-optimal parameters vary across scenes,

  • •

    optimal mixtures lie in the interior of the simplex,

  • •

    token routers lack explicit global scene access.

E.3 Temporal Causality and Cross-Modal Coordination Disruption

We show that token-level routing (Sparse and Soft MoE) structurally disrupts temporal causality and cross-modal coordination in flow-based driving planners, while SAMoE preserves both properties.

Throughout this section we rely on the previously established local bi-Lipschitz property:

Local Bi-Lipschitz Property.

There exist constants L≥c>0L\geq c>0 such that for all θ,θ′∈conv⁡({θ(e)})∩ℛtrain\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in\mathrm{conv}(\{\theta^{(e)}\})\cap\mathcal{R}_{\text{train}},

c​‖θ−θ′‖2≤‖vθ​(x,t)−vθ′​(x,t)‖2≤L​‖θ−θ′‖2.c\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|_{2}\leq\|v_{\theta}(x,t)-v_{\theta^{\prime}}(x,t)\|_{2}\leq L\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|_{2}. (98)

This ensures that parameter perturbations induce proportional perturbations in the vector field.

1. Temporal Causality Disruption

The planner is modeled as a flow-matching ODE:

d​y​(t)d​t=vθt​(y⁡(t),t).\frac{dy(t)}{dt}=v_{\theta_{t}}(y(t),t). (99)
Definition (Temporal Causality).

The model preserves temporal causality if small input perturbations between adjacent timesteps lead to small deviations in the generated trajectory:

‖y1​(t)−y2​(t)‖≤C​‖xt−xt′‖.\|y_{1}(t)-y_{2}(t)\|\leq C\|x_{t}-x_{t}^{\prime}\|. (100)

Sparse Token-Level MoE

Sparse MoE applies discrete Top-kk routing:

Sπt=Top​-​k​(Router⁡(xt)).S_{\pi_{t}}=\mathrm{Top}\text{-}k(\mathrm{Router}(x_{t})). (101)

Because Top-kk is piecewise constant, there exist arbitrarily close inputs xt,xt′x_{t},x_{t}^{\prime} such that

‖xt−xt′‖2→0,θt≠θt′.\|x_{t}-x_{t}^{\prime}\|_{2}\to 0,\qquad\theta_{t}\neq\theta_{t}^{\prime}. (102)

Hence

‖θt−θt′‖2≥δ>0.\|\theta_{t}-\theta_{t}^{\prime}\|_{2}\geq\delta>0. (103)

By the bi-Lipschitz lower bound:

‖vθt​(x,t)−vθt′​(x,t)‖2≥c​δ.\|v_{\theta_{t}}(x,t)-v_{\theta_{t}^{\prime}}(x,t)\|_{2}\geq c\delta. (104)

Thus arbitrarily small input perturbations induce finite jumps in the vector field.

Trajectory-Level Consequence via ODE Stability.

Consider two ODE systems initialized at the same state y1​(0)=y2​(0)y_{1}(0)=y_{2}(0):

d​y1d​t=vθt​(y1​(t),t),d​y2d​t=vθt′​(y2​(t),t).\frac{dy_{1}}{dt}=v_{\theta_{t}}(y_{1}(t),t),\qquad\frac{dy_{2}}{dt}=v_{\theta_{t}^{\prime}}(y_{2}(t),t). (105)

Define the trajectory error

e⁡(t):=y1​(t)−y2​(t).e(t):=y_{1}(t)-y_{2}(t). (106)

Then

d​e​(t)d​t=vθt​(y1,t)−vθt′​(y2,t).\frac{de(t)}{dt}=v_{\theta_{t}}(y_{1},t)-v_{\theta_{t}^{\prime}}(y_{2},t). (107)

Adding and subtracting vθt​(y2,t)v_{\theta_{t}}(y_{2},t) gives

d​e​(t)d​t=vθt​(y1,t)−vθt​(y2,t)⏟(A)+vθt​(y2,t)−vθt′​(y2,t)⏟(B).\frac{de(t)}{dt}=\underbrace{v_{\theta_{t}}(y_{1},t)-v_{\theta_{t}}(y_{2},t)}_{(A)}+\underbrace{v_{\theta_{t}}(y_{2},t)-v_{\theta_{t}^{\prime}}(y_{2},t)}_{(B)}. (108)
State Lipschitz Bound.

Assume the vector field is Lipschitz in the state variable:

‖vθ​(y1,t)−vθ​(y2,t)‖≤Ly​‖y1−y2‖.\|v_{\theta}(y_{1},t)-v_{\theta}(y_{2},t)\|\leq L_{y}\|y_{1}-y_{2}\|. (109)

Thus

‖(A)‖≤Ly​‖e⁡(t)‖.\|(A)\|\leq L_{y}\|e(t)\|. (110)
Parameter-Induced Vector Field Gap.

From the previously established bi-Lipschitz property of the vector field with respect to parameters,

‖vθt​(y,t)−vθt′​(y,t)‖≥c​‖θt−θt′‖.\|v_{\theta_{t}}(y,t)-v_{\theta_{t}^{\prime}}(y,t)\|\geq c\|\theta_{t}-\theta_{t}^{\prime}\|. (111)

If the routing perturbation satisfies

‖θt−θt′‖≥δ,\|\theta_{t}-\theta_{t}^{\prime}\|\geq\delta, (112)

then for any state yy

‖vθt​(y,t)−vθt′​(y,t)‖≥c​δ.\|v_{\theta_{t}}(y,t)-v_{\theta_{t}^{\prime}}(y,t)\|\geq c\delta. (113)

In particular, term (B) satisfies

‖(B)‖≥c​δ.\|(B)\|\geq c\delta. (114)
Early-Time Trajectory Deviation.

At t=0t=0, since y1​(0)=y2​(0)y_{1}(0)=y_{2}(0), we have

d​ed​t​(0)=vθ0​(y0,0)−vθ0′​(y0,0).\frac{de}{dt}(0)=v_{\theta_{0}}(y_{0},0)-v_{\theta_{0}^{\prime}}(y_{0},0). (115)

Therefore

‖d​ed​t​(0)‖≥c​δ.\left\|\frac{de}{dt}(0)\right\|\geq c\delta. (116)

By continuity of the vector field, there exists a small τ>0\tau>0 such that for all t∈[0,τ]t\in[0,\tau]

‖d​ed​t​(t)‖≥c2​δ.\left\|\frac{de}{dt}(t)\right\|\geq\frac{c}{2}\delta. (117)

Integrating over [0,t][0,t] yields

‖e⁡(t)‖=‖∫0td​ed​s​𝑑s‖≥∫0t‖d​ed​s‖​𝑑s≥c2​δ​t.\|e(t)\|=\left\|\int_{0}^{t}\frac{de}{ds}\,ds\right\|\geq\int_{0}^{t}\left\|\frac{de}{ds}\right\|ds\geq\frac{c}{2}\delta t. (118)

Hence for any t∈(0,τ]t\in(0,\tau]

‖y1​(t)−y2​(t)‖≥c2​δ​t.\|y_{1}(t)-y_{2}(t)\|\geq\frac{c}{2}\delta t. (119)
Implication.

Thus even when the input states become arbitrarily close (‖xt−xt′‖→0\|x_{t}-x_{t}^{\prime}\|\to 0), a routing-induced parameter perturbation ‖θt−θt′‖≥δ\|\theta_{t}-\theta_{t}^{\prime}\|\geq\delta leads to a trajectory deviation satisfying

‖y1​(t)−y2​(t)‖≥Ω⁡(δ).\|y_{1}(t)-y_{2}(t)\|\geq\Omega(\delta). (120)

This shows that small routing perturbations can induce non-vanishing trajectory deviations, implying instability at the trajectory level.

Soft Token-Level MoE

Soft MoE removes the discrete Top-kk routing, but the routing remains token-dependent. The effective parameters at time tt become

θt=∑eπe,t​θ(e),\theta_{t}=\sum_{e}\pi_{e,t}\theta^{(e)}, (121)

where πe,t\pi_{e,t} are routing weights satisfying ∑eπe,t=1\sum_{e}\pi_{e,t}=1.

Routing Weight Sensitivity.

The parameter difference between two consecutive timesteps is

θt−θt−1=∑e(πe,t−πe,t−1)​θ(e).\theta_{t}-\theta_{t-1}=\sum_{e}(\pi_{e,t}-\pi_{e,t-1})\theta^{(e)}. (122)

If expert parameters are bounded, there exists a constant c′>0c^{\prime}>0 such that

‖θt−θt−1‖2≥c′​‖πt−πt−1‖2.\|\theta_{t}-\theta_{t-1}\|_{2}\geq c^{\prime}\|\pi_{t}-\pi_{t-1}\|_{2}. (123)
Vector Field Perturbation.

Using the previously established bi-Lipschitz property of the vector field with respect to parameters,

‖vθt​(y,t)−vθt−1​(y,t)‖≥c​‖θt−θt−1‖,\|v_{\theta_{t}}(y,t)-v_{\theta_{t-1}}(y,t)\|\geq c\|\theta_{t}-\theta_{t-1}\|, (124)

which implies

‖vθt​(y,t)−vθt−1​(y,t)‖≥c​c′​‖πt−πt−1‖.\|v_{\theta_{t}}(y,t)-v_{\theta_{t-1}}(y,t)\|\geq cc^{\prime}\|\pi_{t}-\pi_{t-1}\|. (125)
Trajectory Consequence.

Suppose the routing weights vary significantly between consecutive timesteps, i.e.,

‖πt−πt−1‖2≥ϵ\|\pi_{t}-\pi_{t-1}\|_{2}\geq\epsilon (126)

for some ϵ>0\epsilon>0 on a set of timesteps with positive measure. Then the induced vector field perturbation satisfies

‖vθt−vθt−1‖≥c​c′​ϵ.\|v_{\theta_{t}}-v_{\theta_{t-1}}\|\geq cc^{\prime}\epsilon. (127)

Applying the short-time ODE stability argument, the resulting trajectories satisfy

‖y⁡(t)−y′​(t)‖≥Ω⁡(ϵ).\|y(t)-y^{\prime}(t)\|\geq\Omega(\epsilon). (128)
Implication.

In practice, token-level soft routing often exhibits rapid temporal fluctuations in mixture weights due to sensitivity to small variations in token embeddings across frames. Such routing oscillations can propagate through the bi-Lipschitz vector field, leading to non-smooth or jittery trajectory behavior.

2. Cross-Modal Coordination Disruption

Let modalities be indexed by mm. Under token-level MoE routing, each modality produces its own routing weights based on modality-specific tokens. The resulting effective parameters are

θ(m)=∑eπe(m)​θ(e),\theta^{(m)}=\sum_{e}\pi_{e}^{(m)}\theta^{(e)}, (129)

where πe(m)\pi_{e}^{(m)} denotes the routing weight of expert ee for modality mm.

Since routing depends on modality-specific token embeddings, different modalities may produce different routing decisions, leading to

θ(m1)≠θ(m2).\theta^{(m_{1})}\neq\theta^{(m_{2})}. (130)

When modality-specific tokens lead to meaningfully different routing weights, the parameter discrepancy satisfies

‖θ(m1)−θ(m2)‖≥δm\|\theta^{(m_{1})}-\theta^{(m_{2})}\|\geq\delta_{m} (131)

for some δm>0\delta_{m}>0.

Vector Field Discrepancy.

Using the previously established bi-Lipschitz property of the vector field with respect to parameters,

‖vθ(m1)​(y,t)−vθ(m2)​(y,t)‖≥c​δm.\|v_{\theta^{(m_{1})}}(y,t)-v_{\theta^{(m_{2})}}(y,t)\|\geq c\delta_{m}. (132)
Trajectory Consequence.

Consider two trajectories generated from the same initial state but using modality-specific parameters:

d​ym1d​t=vθ(m1)​(ym1,t),d​ym2d​t=vθ(m2)​(ym2,t).\frac{dy_{m_{1}}}{dt}=v_{\theta^{(m_{1})}}(y_{m_{1}},t),\qquad\frac{dy_{m_{2}}}{dt}=v_{\theta^{(m_{2})}}(y_{m_{2}},t). (133)

Applying the same short-time ODE stability argument (Appendix E.1), we obtain

‖ym1​(t)−ym2​(t)‖≥Ω⁡(δm).\|y_{m_{1}}(t)-y_{m_{2}}(t)\|\geq\Omega(\delta_{m}). (134)
Implication.

Therefore, when modality-dependent routing leads to non-negligible parameter discrepancies, the resulting vector field mismatch can induce trajectory-level divergence, potentially disrupting cross-modal coordination in downstream decision-making.

3. Stability of SAMoE

SAMoE performs scene-level parameter merging:

θ⁡(s)=∑eπe​(s)​θ(e).\theta(s)=\sum_{e}\pi_{e}(s)\theta^{(e)}. (135)

All modalities share the same parameter:

θ(m)=θ⁡(s).\theta^{(m)}=\theta(s). (136)

Hence no parameter discrepancy exists across modalities, and cross-modal parameter divergence is eliminated at the source.

Temporal Stability of the Vector Field.

Assume the scene encoder is Lipschitz continuous:

‖θ⁡(st)−θ⁡(st−1)‖2≤Ls​‖st−st−1‖2.\|\theta(s_{t})-\theta(s_{t-1})\|_{2}\leq L_{s}\|s_{t}-s_{t-1}\|_{2}. (137)

Using the upper bound of the local bi-Lipschitz property (98),

‖vθ⁡(st)​(x,t)−vθ⁡(st−1)​(x,t)‖2≤L​‖θ⁡(st)−θ⁡(st−1)‖2,\|v_{\theta(s_{t})}(x,t)-v_{\theta(s_{t-1})}(x,t)\|_{2}\leq L\|\theta(s_{t})-\theta(s_{t-1})\|_{2}, (138)

which yields

‖vθ⁡(st)−vθ⁡(st−1)‖2≤L​Ls​‖st−st−1‖2.\|v_{\theta(s_{t})}-v_{\theta(s_{t-1})}\|_{2}\leq LL_{s}\|s_{t}-s_{t-1}\|_{2}. (139)

Thus the induced vector field is Lipschitz with respect to scene perturbations.

Trajectory-Level Stability via ODE Analysis.

Consider two trajectories generated from scenes sts_{t} and st−1s_{t-1}:

d​y1d​t=vθ⁡(st)​(y1,t),d​y2d​t=vθ⁡(st−1)​(y2,t).\frac{dy_{1}}{dt}=v_{\theta(s_{t})}(y_{1},t),\qquad\frac{dy_{2}}{dt}=v_{\theta(s_{t-1})}(y_{2},t). (140)

Define e⁡(t)=y1​(t)−y2​(t)e(t)=y_{1}(t)-y_{2}(t). Then

d​e​(t)d​t=vθ⁡(st)​(y1,t)−vθ⁡(st−1)​(y2,t).\frac{de(t)}{dt}=v_{\theta(s_{t})}(y_{1},t)-v_{\theta(s_{t-1})}(y_{2},t). (141)

Add and subtract vθ⁡(st)​(y2,t)v_{\theta(s_{t})}(y_{2},t):

d​e​(t)d​t=vθ⁡(st)​(y1,t)−vθ⁡(st)​(y2,t)⏟state Lipschitz+vθ⁡(st)​(y2,t)−vθ⁡(st−1)​(y2,t)⏟scene-induced difference.\frac{de(t)}{dt}=\underbrace{v_{\theta(s_{t})}(y_{1},t)-v_{\theta(s_{t})}(y_{2},t)}_{\text{state Lipschitz}}+\underbrace{v_{\theta(s_{t})}(y_{2},t)-v_{\theta(s_{t-1})}(y_{2},t)}_{\text{scene-induced difference}}. (142)

Using state Lipschitz constant LyL_{y}:

‖(A)‖≤Ly​‖e⁡(t)‖.\|(A)\|\leq L_{y}\|e(t)\|. (143)

Using the vector-field Lipschitz bound above:

‖(B)‖≤L​Ls​‖st−st−1‖.\|(B)\|\leq LL_{s}\|s_{t}-s_{t-1}\|. (144)

Hence

dd​t​‖e⁡(t)‖≤Ly|e⁡(t)|+L​Ls​‖st−st−1‖.\frac{d}{dt}\|e(t)\|\leq L_{y}\|e(t)\|+LL_{s}\|s_{t}-s_{t-1}\|. (145)

Solving this linear differential inequality yields

‖e⁡(t)‖≤L​LsLy​(eLy​t−1)​‖st−st−1‖.\|e(t)\|\leq\frac{LL_{s}}{L_{y}}\left(e^{L_{y}t}-1\right)\|s_{t}-s_{t-1}\|. (146)

Therefore, for finite horizon tt,

‖y1​(t)−y2​(t)‖≤C~​‖st−st−1‖,\|y_{1}(t)-y_{2}(t)\|\leq\tilde{C}\|s_{t}-s_{t-1}\|, (147)

for some constant C~>0\tilde{C}>0.

Conclusion.

Unlike token-level MoE, SAMoE induces a scene-level Lipschitz parameterization. The resulting vector field is Lipschitz continuous, and ODE stability guarantees trajectory continuity.

Hence SAMoE preserves temporal causality and avoids trajectory-level instability.

Theorem E.1 (Trajectory-Level Structural Disruption)

Under local routing, token-level MoE induces parameter discontinuities (Sparse) or oscillations (Soft). By the local bi-Lipschitz mapping and ODE stability, these parameter perturbations propagate into finite trajectory deviations, violating temporal causality and cross-modal coordination.

In contrast, SAMoE maintains continuous scene-level parameterization, thereby preserving trajectory-level stability.

E.4 Convergence Advantage of SAMoE

We analyze optimization convergence under stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Let the training objective be

minθ⁡ℒ⁡(θ),\min_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta), (148)

where ℒ\mathcal{L} is possibly non-convex.

Assumptions.

(A1) ℒ\mathcal{L} is LL-smooth:

‖∇ℒ​(θ1)−∇ℒ​(θ2)‖≤L​‖θ1−θ2‖.\|\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta_{1})-\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta_{2})\|\leq L\|\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\|. (149)

(A2) The stochastic gradient gtg_{t} satisfies

𝔼⁡[gt|θt]=∇ℒ​(θt),\mathbb{E}[g_{t}|\theta_{t}]=\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta_{t}), (150)
𝔼​‖gt−∇ℒ​(θt)‖2≤σ2.\mathbb{E}\|g_{t}-\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta_{t})\|^{2}\leq\sigma^{2}. (151)
SGD Descent Inequality.

SGD update:

θt+1=θt−η​gt.\theta_{t+1}=\theta_{t}-\eta g_{t}. (152)

By LL-smoothness,

ℒ⁡(θt+1)≤ℒ⁡(θt)−η⁡⟨∇ℒ​(θt),gt⟩+L​η22​‖gt‖2.\mathcal{L}(\theta_{t+1})\leq\mathcal{L}(\theta_{t})-\eta\langle\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta_{t}),g_{t}\rangle+\frac{L\eta^{2}}{2}\|g_{t}\|^{2}. (153)

Taking expectation and using the variance bound yields

𝔼⁡[ℒ⁡(θt+1)]≤ℒ⁡(θt)−η2​‖∇ℒ​(θt)‖2+L​η22​σ2,\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}(\theta_{t+1})]\leq\mathcal{L}(\theta_{t})-\frac{\eta}{2}\|\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta_{t})\|^{2}+\frac{L\eta^{2}}{2}\sigma^{2}, (154)

for η≤1/L\eta\leq 1/L.

Summing over t=0,…,T−1t=0,\dots,T-1 gives

1T​∑t=0T−1𝔼​‖∇ℒ​(θt)‖2≤2​(ℒ⁡(θ0)−ℒ∗)η​T+L​η​σ2.\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta_{t})\|^{2}\leq\frac{2(\mathcal{L}(\theta_{0})-\mathcal{L}^{*})}{\eta T}+L\eta\sigma^{2}. (155)

Choosing η=O⁡(1/T)\eta=O(1/\sqrt{T}) yields

1T​∑t=0T−1𝔼​‖∇ℒ​(θt)‖2=O⁡(1T)+O⁡(σ2T).\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\mathcal{L}(\theta_{t})\|^{2}=O\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\right)+O\!\left(\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\sqrt{T}}\right). (156)

Therefore, the convergence behavior depends critically on the stochastic gradient variance σ2\sigma^{2}.

Routing-Induced Gradient Variance.

In MoE models, the effective parameter depends on the input:

θ⁡(x)=∑eπe​(x)​θ(e).\theta(x)=\sum_{e}\pi_{e}(x)\theta^{(e)}. (157)

Consequently the gradient variance decomposes as

σ2=σdata2+σrouting2,\sigma^{2}=\sigma^{2}_{\text{data}}+\sigma^{2}_{\text{routing}}, (158)

where σrouting2\sigma^{2}_{\text{routing}} arises from variation of the effective parameter θ⁡(x)\theta(x) within a mini-batch.

We quantify this term via parameter dispersion

σrouting2∝𝔼​‖θ⁡(x)−θ¯‖2,\sigma^{2}_{\text{routing}}\propto\mathbb{E}\|\theta(x)-\bar{\theta}\|^{2}, (159)

where θ¯\bar{\theta} is the batch-mean parameter.

Theorem E.2 (Variance Reduction of Scene-Level Routing)

Under Assumptions (A1)-(A2), SGD satisfies the bound (155). Moreover, routing mechanisms with lower parameter dispersion 𝔼​‖θ⁡(x)−θ¯‖2\mathbb{E}\|\theta(x)-\bar{\theta}\|^{2} lead to smaller gradient variance σrouting2\sigma^{2}_{\text{routing}} and thus a tighter SGD bound.

In practice, the routing variance typically follows the qualitative ordering

σSparse2≳σSoft2≳σSAMoE2.\sigma^{2}_{\text{Sparse}}\;\gtrsim\;\sigma^{2}_{\text{Soft}}\;\gtrsim\;\sigma^{2}_{\text{SAMoE}}. (160)

Therefore scene-level routing as used in SAMoE reduces routing-induced gradient variance and improves optimization stability.

Proof Sketch.

Step 1: Variance Decomposition.

Let the stochastic gradient be

g⁡(x)=∇θℓ​(θ⁡(x),x).g(x)=\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta(x);x). (161)

Assume the gradient is Lipschitz in θ\theta:

‖∇θℓ​(θ1,x)−∇θℓ​(θ2,x)‖≤G​‖θ1−θ2‖.\|\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{1};x)-\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{2};x)\|\leq G\|\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\|. (162)

Then routing variance satisfies

σrouting2≤G2​𝔼​‖θ⁡(x)−θ¯‖2.\sigma^{2}_{\text{routing}}\leq G^{2}\mathbb{E}\|\theta(x)-\bar{\theta}\|^{2}. (163)

Thus gradient variance is controlled by parameter dispersion.

Step 2: Sparse MoE.

For Top-kk routing,

θ⁡(x)=∑e∈Sπ⁡(x)θ(e).\theta(x)=\sum_{e\in S_{\pi(x)}}\theta^{(e)}. (164)

Because routing decisions are discrete, the mapping x↦θ⁡(x)x\mapsto\theta(x) is piecewise constant. Small input perturbations can therefore cause abrupt changes in expert selection.

In heterogeneous mini-batches spanning multiple routing regions, such discontinuities may produce large variation in effective parameters θ⁡(x)\theta(x) across samples, leading to increased routing variance.

Step 3: Soft MoE.

Soft MoE replaces discrete routing with continuous mixture weights:

θ⁡(x)=∑eπe​(x)​θ(e).\theta(x)=\sum_{e}\pi_{e}(x)\theta^{(e)}. (165)

The mapping x↦θ⁡(x)x\mapsto\theta(x) is therefore continuous, removing jump discontinuities in parameter assignments. Although mixture weights may still vary across tokens, parameter dispersion is typically smaller than in sparse Top-kk routing.

Step 4: SAMoE.

SAMoE performs routing at the scene level:

θ⁡(s)=∑eπe​(s)​θ(e).\theta(s)=\sum_{e}\pi_{e}(s)\theta^{(e)}. (166)

All tokens within the same scene share the same parameter. Assume the scene encoder is Lipschitz:

‖θ⁡(si)−θ⁡(sj)‖≤Ls​‖si−sj‖.\|\theta(s_{i})-\theta(s_{j})\|\leq L_{s}\|s_{i}-s_{j}\|. (167)

In driving scenarios, scene embeddings are typically computed from aggregated multi-modal features (e.g., BEV representations or pooled token features). Such aggregated representations exhibit substantially lower variance across tokens within the same frame than individual token embeddings.

Consequently parameter dispersion satisfies

𝔼​‖θ⁡(s)−θ¯‖2≤Ls2​Var​(s),\mathbb{E}\|\theta(s)-\bar{\theta}\|^{2}\leq L_{s}^{2}\mathrm{Var}(s), (168)

which is typically smaller than token-level dispersion.

Conclusion.

Scene-level routing reduces intra-batch parameter variation, leading to smaller routing-induced gradient variance. Substituting this into the SGD bound (155) yields a tighter optimization bound, which empirically translates to more stable and often faster convergence during training.

E.5 Gradient Stability of SAMoE.

We now analyze the intrinsic gradient stability of SAMoE. The goal is to show that the stochastic gradient varies in a controlled and Lipschitz manner with respect to scene variation.

Setting.

In SAMoE, the effective parameter is scene-dependent:

θ⁡(s)=∑eπe​(s)​θ(e),\theta(s)=\sum_{e}\pi_{e}(s)\theta^{(e)}, (169)

where ss denotes the scene representation, and all tokens within the same scene share the same θ⁡(s)\theta(s).

Let the per-sample loss be ℓ⁡(θ⁡(s),x)\ell(\theta(s);x).

Assumptions.

(A1) The loss gradient is Lipschitz in the parameter:

‖∇θℓ​(θ1,x)−∇θℓ​(θ2,x)‖≤G​‖θ1−θ2‖.\|\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{1};x)-\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta_{2};x)\|\leq G\|\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\|. (170)

(A2) The scene-conditioned parameter mapping is Lipschitz:

‖θ⁡(s1)−θ⁡(s2)‖≤Ls​‖s1−s2‖.\|\theta(s_{1})-\theta(s_{2})\|\leq L_{s}\|s_{1}-s_{2}\|. (171)

Proposition (Gradient Stability of SAMoE).

Under (A1)-(A2), the gradient field of SAMoE satisfies

‖∇θℓ​(θ⁡(s1),x)−∇θℓ​(θ⁡(s2),x)‖≤G​Ls​‖s1−s2‖.\|\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta(s_{1});x)-\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta(s_{2});x)\|\leq GL_{s}\|s_{1}-s_{2}\|. (172)

Proof.

By Assumption (A1),

‖∇θℓ​(θ⁡(s1),x)−∇θℓ​(θ⁡(s2),x)‖≤G​‖θ⁡(s1)−θ⁡(s2)‖.\|\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta(s_{1});x)-\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta(s_{2});x)\|\leq G\|\theta(s_{1})-\theta(s_{2})\|. (173)

Applying Assumption (A2),

‖θ⁡(s1)−θ⁡(s2)‖≤Ls​‖s1−s2‖.\|\theta(s_{1})-\theta(s_{2})\|\leq L_{s}\|s_{1}-s_{2}\|. (174)

Combining the two inequalities yields

‖∇θℓ​(θ⁡(s1),x)−∇θℓ​(θ⁡(s2),x)‖≤G​Ls​‖s1−s2‖.\|\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta(s_{1});x)-\nabla_{\theta}\ell(\theta(s_{2});x)\|\leq GL_{s}\|s_{1}-s_{2}\|. (175)

□\square

Implications.

Equation (172) shows that the gradient field of SAMoE is Lipschitz continuous with constant G​LsGL_{s} with respect to scene variation.

This implies:

1. Small perturbations in scene representation lead to proportionally small gradient changes.

2. The gradient does not exhibit abrupt jumps.

3. The stochastic optimization trajectory evolves under a smooth vector field.

Consequently, SAMoE enjoys intrinsically stable gradient dynamics during training.

F Algorithm

G Challenging Scenarios: Selection from nuScenes

To evaluate the behavior and safety of token-level Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) mechanisms in embodied driving, we construct three focused subsets from the nuScenes corpus that emphasize scene-level difficulties underrepresented in the full dataset. The selection is quantitative and metric-driven: for each sample we compute per-sample statistics (agent count, yaw rate, and minimum inter-agent distance) over the full split (N = 34,149) and apply simple, interpretable thresholds to isolate challenging examples.

G.1 Selection criteria

The three subsets target distinct failure modes relevant to scene-level decision-making:

  • •

    Complex intersection (high agent density). Samples with average agent count >40>40 to capture scenes with many traffic participants and high interaction complexity.

  • •

    Narrow turning (high maneuvering). Samples with average yaw rate >0.05​rad/s>0.05\ \mathrm{rad/s} to capture aggressive or complex turning trajectories.

  • •

    Close overtake (close proximity). Samples with average minimum inter-agent distance <8​m<8\ \mathrm{m} to capture scenarios requiring tight spacing, braking, or precise lateral control.

G.2 Subset statistics

Table 5 summarizes the resulting subsets and the full nuScenes statistics used for thresholding.

These subsets are deliberately rare in the full corpus: List 1 comprises 38/34149≈0.1113%38/34149\approx 0.1113\%, List 2 comprises 27/34149≈0.0791%27/34149\approx 0.0791\%, and List 3 comprises 42/34149≈0.1230%42/34149\approx 0.1230\%. Relative to the dataset averages, the subsets deviate markedly in the intended directions: List 1 contains ≈1.53×\approx 1.53\times the mean agent count, List 2 exhibits a yaw rate of ≈5.15×\approx 5.15\times the dataset mean, and List 3’s minimum inter-agent distance is ≈0.72×\approx 0.72\times the dataset mean (a reduction of ≈2.29​m\approx 2.29\ \mathrm{m}). These deltas confirm that the chosen thresholds successfully isolate denser, more dynamic, and closer-proximity interactions respectively.

G.3 Evaluation protocol

For each subset we generate closed-loop trajectories and report the following metrics:

  • •

    L2 error: Euclidean distance between predicted and ground-truth trajectories (m).

  • •

    Collision rate: Fraction of trajectories incurring any collision during the evaluation rollout.

  • •

    Success rate: Fraction of trajectories satisfying both L2 error <0.4​m<0.4\ \mathrm{m} and zero collisions.

These metrics quantify tracking fidelity, safety, and task completion under challenging scene-level constraints.

G.4 Motivation and expected value

Typical nuScenes driving frames are dominated by relatively straightforward motion; therefore, aggregate evaluations can mask failure modes that emerge only under strong scene-level interactions. The targeted subsets act as a discriminative benchmark to reveal whether token-level MoE routing—originally developed for tokenized language modeling—can robustly support scene-level, safety-critical decision-making in autonomous driving. Consequently, improvements observed on these subsets provide stronger evidence that a method meaningfully enhances performance in complex, safety-relevant scenarios beyond gains on the dataset average.

H More Qualitative Results

This section presents additional qualitative driving scenarios to further evaluate the scene-adaptive capability of our MoE-enabled model. These cases span diverse and safety-critical environments, including signalized intersections, narrow urban lanes, multi-lane roadways, and highly interactive scenes involving both vehicles and pedestrians.

Scene-adaptive behavior across diverse maneuvers. As illustrated in Fig. 10–15, our model demonstrates consistent controllability in a wide range of maneuvers, such as waiting at a red-light queue (Fig. 10), making safe left and right turns through narrow or constrained lanes (Fig. 11, Fig. 12, Fig. 15), approaching complex multi-lane intersections (Fig. 13), and performing lane-change maneuvers near blocked traffic (Fig. 14). In all these settings, the predicted trajectories closely follow the ground-truth motion, avoiding collisions and adapting to the dynamic constraints of each scene.

Effectiveness of MoE in complex interactive scenarios. We further compare the MoE-enabled model with the non-MoE baseline in challenging scenes exhibiting strong multi-agent interactions and structural constraints. As shown in Fig. 16, the MoE model successfully reasons about lane geometry and traffic flows, producing a valid straight-driving trajectory, whereas the non-MoE model deviates into an invalid region. Similarly, in dense right-turn scenarios with close-proximity vehicles (Fig. 17), the MoE model maintains accurate predictions over time, while the non-MoE baseline accumulates substantial errors. These results highlight the model’s superior ability to integrate scene understanding and trajectory prediction, especially under complex and highly interactive conditions.

I Additional Computational Efficiency and Deployment Analysis

To complement the planning accuracy and closed-loop evaluations presented in the main paper, we further analyze the computational efficiency and memory characteristics of the proposed Scene-Adaptive MoE (SA-MoE) under a realistic deployment setting. Considering the practical constraints of autonomous driving systems, all measurements are conducted on a single GPU with mixed-precision inference (FP16), which reflects a single-card on-vehicle or edge deployment scenario rather than multi-GPU data-center configurations.

I.1 Experimental Setup

We benchmark three modules under identical configurations: (i) a conventional token-level sparse MoE block, (ii) the proposed scene-adaptive soft-weighted SA-MoE layer, and (iii) a single expert block extracted from the MoE architecture for reference. All results report average inference latency, token throughput, estimated FLOPs, and GPU memory statistics.

I.2 Latency and Throughput Comparison

Under identical parameter budgets (∼\sim276M parameters), the conventional sparse MoE block achieves an average inference time of 46.1746.17 ms with a throughput of 44,35644{,}356 tokens/s. In contrast, SA-MoE reduces latency to 43.8943.89 ms and increases throughput to 46,66746{,}667 tokens/s, yielding a relative speedup of 1.05×1.05\times.

Although the parameter counts are nearly identical (276.84M vs. 276.83M), SA-MoE achieves substantially lower computational cost per token. The estimated FLOPs per token decrease from 6.92×1076.92\times 10^{7} (sparse MoE) to 3.51×1073.51\times 10^{7} (SA-MoE), corresponding to a 1.97×1.97\times reduction. This reduction arises because SA-MoE performs expert weight fusion once per layer and executes a single merged FFN, whereas token-level sparse routing activates multiple experts per token and incurs additional routing overhead.

I.3 Memory Behavior

A notable difference appears in memory allocation patterns. The sparse MoE block exhibits a memory increase of 47.847.8 MB during inference, while SA-MoE shows only 0.20.2 MB additional steady-state memory usage. The relative steady-state memory delta is thus reduced by over two orders of magnitude.

Although SA-MoE records a higher transient CUDA peak memory (due to temporary expert weight merging buffers), the post-execution memory footprint returns to the same level as the sparse MoE implementation. This behavior indicates that SA-MoE does not increase persistent deployment memory requirements, which is critical for embedded automotive hardware.

I.4 Computational Analysis of the Deformable Scene Encoder (Router Module)

We further isolate and benchmark the Deformable Scene Encoder (DSE), which serves as the scene-adaptive routing module in SA-MoE. This component is responsible for extracting BEV-conditioned routing representations and generating expert fusion weights. Since routing is computed once per forward pass and reused across transformer layers, its computational overhead is critical for real-time deployment.

Under the same single-GPU mixed-precision (FP16) setting, the DSE module contains 23.0723.07M parameters. The average inference latency is measured at 2.8832.883 ms, corresponding to a throughput of 710,323710{,}323 tokens per second.

The estimated total FLOPs of the DSE forward pass are 4.73×10104.73\times 10^{10}, yielding approximately 2.31×1072.31\times 10^{7} FLOPs per token. Although the absolute FLOP count appears non-negligible, it is important to emphasize that DSE is executed only once per planning step and its output is reused across all SA-MoE layers. Consequently, its amortized per-layer computational contribution remains small.

In terms of memory behavior, no measurable persistent memory increase is observed (0.0 MB delta between pre- and post-execution states). The CUDA peak memory reaches 1168.31168.3 MB during execution and returns to 1124.31124.3 MB afterward, indicating that temporary buffers are released properly and that DSE introduces no additional steady-state memory burden.

These results confirm that the Deformable Scene Encoder introduces minimal latency and negligible persistent memory overhead, validating the design choice of scene-level routing. The router remains computationally lightweight relative to the full planning expert, making SA-MoE suitable for single-card autonomous driving deployment scenarios.

I.5 Hardware-Aware Efficiency Analysis under Autonomous Driving Deployment for SA-MoE

While Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures have become a standard scaling strategy in large language models (LLMs), their design is typically optimized for large-scale distributed training and inference environments. In most LLM deployments, MoE layers are executed across multiple GPUs or nodes, where different experts are distributed across devices and token routing is implemented through collective communication primitives such as all-to-all. This distributed setting allows sparse expert activation to reduce the effective compute per token while maintaining large model capacity.

However, the deployment constraints of autonomous driving systems differ fundamentally from those of large-scale cloud inference. Production autonomous vehicles typically operate under strict hardware budgets and latency constraints, where perception, planning, and control modules must share limited computational resources. In practice, most autonomous driving stacks are deployed on a single high-performance GPU (e.g., automotive-grade NVIDIA platforms), rather than multi-GPU clusters. Under this hardware regime, the efficiency characteristics of conventional MoE architectures change significantly.

In token-level sparse MoE designs, such as those commonly used in LLMs, routing decisions are made independently for each token and each layer. Although only a subset of experts is activated per token, the system must still compute routing scores and dynamically gather expert outputs at the token granularity. When executed on a single GPU, this leads to several inefficiencies. First, token-wise dynamic routing introduces irregular memory access patterns and kernel fragmentation, which reduce GPU utilization. Second, repeated routing computation across layers increases control overhead. Third, the fine-grained dispatch mechanism prevents efficient batching of expert computations, limiting the throughput benefits that sparse activation aims to achieve.

Soft MoE methods partially alleviate routing instability by replacing discrete expert selection with soft weighted aggregation. Nevertheless, Soft MoE still operates at the token level and requires computing outputs for multiple experts simultaneously before aggregation. As a result, the computational cost remains close to dense MoE in practice, and the hardware efficiency improvements are limited under single-device deployment.

In contrast, the proposed Scene-Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts (SA-MoE) is explicitly designed with the hardware characteristics of autonomous driving platforms in mind. Instead of performing token-level routing, SA-MoE introduces a scene-level routing mechanism implemented by the Deformable Scene Encoder (DSE). The router processes the BEV scene representation once that are shared across tokens within the planning module. This design leads to several practical advantages.

First, routing overhead is amortized across the entire sequence. Since the routing weights are computed per scene rather than per token, the total routing computation becomes negligible relative to the expert networks themselves. As demonstrated in the empirical analysis, the DSE module introduces only 2.8832.883 ms of latency with 23.0723.07M parameters, representing a small fraction of the total MoE computation.

Second, expert computation becomes structurally regular. Because all tokens share the same scene-level expert mixture, the forward pass can be implemented as a deterministic weighted combination of experts rather than dynamic token dispatch. This eliminates the need for token-wise gather/scatter operations and improves GPU kernel efficiency, particularly on single-device inference.

Third, memory behavior becomes more predictable. Token-level sparse MoE often requires temporary buffers for token regrouping and expert batching, which increases peak memory consumption and fragmentation. In contrast, SA-MoE maintains stable memory usage since expert outputs are computed in-place and fused using precomputed scene-level weights.

These hardware-aware design choices align naturally with the computational constraints of autonomous driving systems. While traditional LLM MoE architectures assume multi-device distributed environments, SA-MoE targets the realistic deployment scenario where Mixture of Experts must run on a single GPU with strict real-time requirements. To further understand the practical efficiency difference between conventional sparse MoE and the proposed SA-MoE under autonomous driving deployment, we analyze the computational behavior from the perspective of a typical automotive GPU platform. Modern autonomous driving systems are commonly deployed on embedded GPU accelerators such as the NVIDIA Orin series, which provides approximately 275275 TOPS of AI compute with 3232 GB LPDDR5 memory bandwidth of roughly 204204 GB/s. In contrast to large-scale LLM serving infrastructure, such platforms operate under a single-device constraint, meaning all experts and routing logic must reside on the same GPU and execute sequentially or partially concurrently.

In conventional sparse MoE architectures, the feed-forward layer is replaced with NN experts, and each token activates the top-kk experts through a routing function. Formally, the output of a sparse MoE layer can be written as

yi=∑j∈TopK​(g​(xi))gj​(xi)​Ej​(xi),y_{i}=\sum_{j\in\text{TopK}(g(x_{i}))}g_{j}(x_{i})\,E_{j}(x_{i}),

where xix_{i} denotes the ii-th token representation, Ej​(⋅)E_{j}(\cdot) is the jj-th expert network, and gj​(xi)g_{j}(x_{i}) is the router weight. Although only kk experts contribute to the final output for each token, the system must still maintain all NN experts in GPU memory and dynamically dispatch tokens to the selected experts.

Under single-GPU execution, this routing mechanism leads to a fundamental hardware inefficiency. Since tokens routed to different experts are typically interleaved within the sequence, the GPU must either (1) perform repeated kernel launches for each expert or (2) reorganize tokens through gather/scatter operations before batched computation. In both cases, all experts must be resident in memory and participate in the scheduling process, which introduces additional overhead in both memory bandwidth and kernel execution.

Let the hidden dimension be dd and the intermediate FFN dimension be mm. The computational cost of a single expert can be approximated as

FLOPsexpert≈2​d​m.\text{FLOPs}_{\text{expert}}\approx 2dm.

For a sparse MoE layer with NN experts and top-kk routing, the theoretical compute per token is

FLOPssparse≈k⋅2​d​m.\text{FLOPs}_{\text{sparse}}\approx k\cdot 2dm.

However, in a single-GPU environment, the effective runtime cost is closer to

FLOPsruntime≈k⋅2​d​m+𝒪⁡(N⋅d),\text{FLOPs}_{\text{runtime}}\approx k\cdot 2dm+\mathcal{O}(N\cdot d),

where the second term represents routing, token dispatch, and memory movement overhead proportional to the total number of experts. As NN increases, this overhead becomes increasingly dominant because each expert must remain resident in GPU memory and participate in the routing pipeline.

In contrast, the proposed SA-MoE replaces token-level routing with scene-level expert fusion. The routing weights are computed once using the Deformable Scene Encoder (DSE), producing a scene-conditioned expert mixture

yi=∑j=1Nαj​(s)​Ej​(xi),y_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\alpha_{j}(s)\,E_{j}(x_{i}),

where ss denotes the scene representation and αj​(s)\alpha_{j}(s) are normalized fusion weights. Since the mixture weights are shared across tokens, expert outputs can be computed sequentially or fused efficiently without dynamic token dispatch.

Under this formulation, the routing complexity becomes independent of the token sequence length:

FLOPsrouter≈𝒪⁡(ds​d),\text{FLOPs}_{\text{router}}\approx\mathcal{O}(d_{s}d),

where dsd_{s} is the BEV scene feature dimension. In our implementation, the router module (DSE) contains only 23.0723.07M parameters and introduces an average latency of 2.8832.883 ms, which is negligible relative to the full MoE computation.

More importantly, the removal of token-level routing eliminates the gather/scatter overhead and irregular memory access patterns that degrade GPU utilization. On single-device inference hardware, this leads to more efficient kernel execution and improved throughput. Empirically, as shown in the performance analysis, SA-MoE achieves approximately 1.05×1.05\times lower latency and nearly 2×2\times reduction in FLOPs per token compared to the baseline sparse MoE block, while maintaining nearly identical parameter capacity.

From a system perspective, this design better aligns with the hardware constraints of embedded autonomous driving platforms. While traditional sparse MoE architectures are optimized for distributed multi-GPU inference, SA-MoE leverages scene-level routing to reduce dynamic scheduling overhead, enabling more efficient execution on a single GPU accelerator.
